cia-0000109057: Cuban Subversive Activities in Latin America: 1959-1968 is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000109057, dated January 5, 1968. cia-0000126957: A November 1965 CIA report gives the short-term political prospects in Panama. The canal made every turn in Panamanian politics Washington's business, and the country's affairs ran through the Canal Zone. The paper forecasts the political weather ahead for that small, watched state. Canal politics gave every Panamanian election an American echo, and short-term forecasts like this one served officials who managed the zone and its treaty questions.
cia-0000132757: Plans by the Cuban government to draw President Eisenhower further in fill a CIA item dated May 5, 1960. Its headline breaks off at the name Eisenho, short for the president. Havana was pulling the American leader into its public campaign that spring. Each clash gave Castro fresh material for speeches at home. The short item reports the plans as analysts heard them.
cia-0000135857: From the CIA files comes a cable dated 6 January 1954, long since declassified, on cable traffic for PBSUCCESS being compromised. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136157: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 5 April 1954, covers team themes for KUGOWN, the talking points handed to the propaganda teams in the field. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136257: The record dated 6 May 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a possible need for bomb support to swing the army, bombing meant to break its loyalty. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136857: Headquarters does not concur with a LINCOLN recommendation in this 1954 cable, because of the Caracas conference. If the source called LIONIZER goes out on a limb and the conference flops, he will be completely discredited hemisphere-wide as a trustworthy source and become only a joke. Instead, headquarters suggests he denounce current Guatemalan-Moscow status, plead for positive action by delegates, and send letters to former Latin American contacts. The cable protects a propaganda voice by keeping his predictions safe.
cia-0000136957: The Secretary of State's morning statement is relayed in this May 1954 cable. It went to the Guatemala City station, with orders to exploit it. He said most Guatemalans want the communists cleaned out. But they face intense communist terrorism, he said. He noted reports of an army ultimatum to Arbenz. He named no sources for those reports. He neither confirmed nor denied a foreign ministers' conference. The station should invite attention to the statement. It would validate the station's own guidance.
un-ga-res-a-69-57:
Arms tipped with depleted uranium leave a residue that worries states where such rounds were fired. Resolution A/69/57, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, takes up the question. It recalls votes on the point since 2007. Views of states and of world bodies on the use of such arms and rounds are noted, as sent to the Secretary-General over the years.

The text gives weight to the counsel of three agencies: the atomic energy body, the UN environment arm, and the World Health Organization. Their shared line is to cut the risk to people and to the land from ground fouled by uranium dust. The vote asks that such counsel be put to work where it fits.
un-sc-res-57: Murder in Jerusalem shocked the Security Council into Resolution 57, passed on 18 September 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte, the UN mediator in Palestine, had been shot dead the day before. A band of gunmen in the city killed him, while he was on his peace work in the Holy Land. The text calls the act cowardly, and the work of a criminal group of terror. The UN flag must fly at half-mast for three days. All costs of the death and burial fall to the UN's funds.
un-sc-res-357: Numbered 357 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1974 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-757: One entry in the Council's numbered series is Resolution 757, catalogued for 1992 by this library. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1557: Security Council Resolution 1557, from 2004, is preserved here in the record wording supplied by English Wikisource. A reader meets the Council's usual order of business: what came before, what the members found, and what they then decided. Keeping the whole text, rather than a digest, is what makes the entry useful for checking claims.
plos-pone-0000057:
Sebastian Graefe, Thomas Streichert, Birgit Budde, and co-authors hunted genes behind resistance to Chagas disease in a 2006 paper. Trypanosoma cruzi, a parasite spread by insects, causes Chagas, which can damage the heart for life. Some mouse strains resist the parasite; others fall ill. The difference lies in susceptibility loci, regions of the genome.

The team found genes from those loci that are switched on differently in resistant mice. Those genes are candidates accounting for the resistant mice's impaired immunity, the odd cost that can come with resisting this parasite. Candidates like these are where drug and vaccine work starts: named genes, in named places, doing measurable things.
cia-0000137457: Filed in Spanish in 1961, document 0000137457 is one of the papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force trained by the CIA for the Bay of Pigs landing that April. The record gives no subject line beyond the brigade file it sits in, so its contents should not be guessed at. It survives as a declassified page of that operation's archive, released through the CIA Reading Room, in the language most of the brigade's own paperwork used.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d57: General George Marshall, Chief of Staff of the Army, wrote to Admiral William Leahy, the President's Chief of Staff, on October 25, 1943. The letter is Document 57 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Staff chiefs writing to each other carried the military side of summit planning while the diplomats met in Moscow. The record names the two soldiers and the date. Its subject rests in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d157: Kirk wrote on November 21, 1943 to Nahas, Egypt's prime minister and foreign minister, and the letter is Document 157 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired with his note to the royal cabinet chief the same day, it shows the American minister working both doors of the host government on the conference's eve. The record gives the names and the date. The letter rests in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d257:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 23 November 1943, met at half past two in the afternoon. They take up China's role in the defeat of Japan under paper C.C.S. 405. General Stilwell opens with word from Chiang Kai-shek that no Chinese proposals should be laid before the chiefs until he has talked again with Roosevelt and Marshall.

Sir Alan Brooke and Admiral Leahy judge the first four proposals in the paper workable, and the rest unrealistic for now. Formosa is singled out: it could not be attacked from the Chinese mainland without landing craft. General Marshall urges care and sympathy anyway, noting that Chiang, long reluctant to build ground forces, now shows real interest in them for the first time. Admiral King agrees the Generalissimo should not be discouraged if that can be avoided.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d357:
Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 28 November 1943 record a morning session at half past eleven. The American chiefs weighed British wishes against Overlord. The first plenary session with Stalin was only hours away. President Roosevelt opens the discussion himself.

Roosevelt understands the British think Allied forces in Italy can reach the Pisa-Rimini line. General Marshall lays out the costs of the rival path. Advancing to Ancona and taking Rhodes in February would push Overlord back to about 15 June, perhaps July. Rhodes would suck in considerable means. The British want Rhodes in place of the Andaman operation, and Turkey's entry above all, claiming Bulgaria and Romania would then fall. Marshall doubts the Straits could open for six to eight months even so, and argues for backing Eisenhower without unduly delaying Overlord.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d457:
Closing day at Cairo also brought a further session of the Combined Chiefs of Staff on December 6, 1943, with minutes printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The chiefs, top American and British officers, had spent the conference turning the Tehran agreements into a workable common strategy. Their meetings ran alongside those of Roosevelt and Churchill.

The session record follows the standard form: who was present, what was raised, and what was decided. Its interest lies in timing as much as content, since a final session shows which questions were still open when the conference broke up. Paired with the day's agreed minutes, it completes the official picture.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d557:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on March 4, 1944, continuing a run of messages across the first days of March. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, in the follow-up correspondence to the conferences.

Churchill's March letters pressed the business of a coalition approaching its greatest operation: the cross-Channel invasion fixed at Tehran for the late spring. Around that fixed point circled arguments about Italy, the Balkans, and relations with France and Russia. For readers, the message is one more turn of the handle by a prime minister who believed that writing itself was a form of command.
frus-1944-quebec-d57:
September 6, 1944 found Churchill writing to Roosevelt once more. He was on the last stage of his Atlantic crossing. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Churchill reached North America that week. He then traveled on to Quebec. The conference there would open on September 12. His letters ahead of arrival staked out Britain's needs. Britain wanted a voice in the Pacific war. It wanted fair terms for continued American aid. It also wanted agreement on Germany. For readers, the message shows him arriving in writing first. He reached Quebec in person days later.
frus-1944-quebec-d157:
Roosevelt settled the French Indochina question for the moment with a short memorandum to Hull on August 28, 1944. The British ambassador's proposals, and the French Committee's aide-mémoire behind them, would wait. The president planned to meet Churchill at Quebec, and he intended the matter to be deferred until after that meeting.

One reason for caution appears in his final line. French participation in planning political warfare in the Far East, Roosevelt noted, involved one of the principal partners: China. Indochina lay in the China theater, and Chiang Kai-shek's views could not be bypassed. Hull was also told orally that the president would raise the French proposals with Churchill directly.
frus-1944-quebec-d257:
On September 13, 1944, the United States Chiefs recommended the Combined Chiefs send General Wilson their own draft message rather than the British one. The approved text, dispatched as Fan 415, gave Wilson two decisions for his future planning in Italy. Both responded directly to his requests for guidance in Naf 774.

First, there would be no withdrawals of major units from the Fifth Army until the outcome of Alexander's present offensive was known. Second, for the capture of the Istrian Peninsula, Wilson could count on the amphibious lift then in the Mediterranean. He was to prepare the operation as soon as possible and submit his plan to the Combined Chiefs by October 10 at the latest.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d57:
Secretary of State Edward Stettinius cabled Ambassador Averell Harriman in Moscow on 15 January 1945. The cable lists who would travel with him to the conference the Americans code-named Argonaut. It was sent by Navy channels and is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta.

Along with Charles Bohlen, Stettinius names H. Freeman Matthews and Alger Hiss, who would handle Dumbarton Oaks matters. Four secretaries and a military aide chosen by General Marshall complete the party. He also asks Harriman to bring stenographer Nelson Newton to help Bohlen write the minutes. Harriman instead brought Edward Page Jr., as the editors' note explains.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d157:
Poland's western frontier kept growing on Soviet maps, Harriman warned on 19 December 1944. His secret cable from Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, tracks how Moscow's offer to Poland had widened in a few months. He writes that he is somewhat concerned by the expanding concept.

At first the Soviets spoke of East Prussia, less Königsberg, and a frontier perhaps as far as the Oder, with Stettin and Breslau thrown in. Then the Oder line hardened into the settled intention. Talking with de Gaulle, Stalin pushed further: the Oder to the lower Neisse, then south along the Neisse to the Czech border near Görlitz. A Pravda article had confirmed the new line in print.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d257:
General Deane sent the Joint Chiefs Stalin's shopping list on 17 October 1944. His cable from the American military mission in Moscow, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, records the night's meeting with Stalin, Molotov, and General Antonov. The list prices Soviet entry into the Pacific war.

Stalin first handed over the supplies America must furnish for a two months' stock in the Far East. Fuel leads: 120,000 tons of high-octane gasoline, 70,000 of motor gasoline, and collapsible storage tanks. Foodstuffs run to some 180,000 tons. Then come 30,000 trucks, 500 amphibious jeeps, 400 C-47 and 100 C-54 aircraft, and naval craft from frigates to sub-chasers. Railroad needs close the list: 500 locomotives, thousands of cars, and some 800 kilometers of rail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d357:
Exact words matter in this American paper of February 6, 1945, which prints the proposed voting formula for the Security Council. The formula had gone to Stalin and Churchill on December 5, 1944. Each member of the council would have one vote. Routine decisions would need seven affirmative votes.

All other decisions would also need seven votes, including the concurring votes of the permanent members. A study of the formula's effects follows the text. This was the heart of the Yalta bargain on the United Nations: great powers kept a veto on action, but not on debate. The paper preserves the wording that made the San Francisco conference possible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d457:
Stalin's dinner on February 10, 1945, ranged from reparations to Jewish problems, and Bohlen's minutes record the talk. Churchill opened with a toast to the King of England, the President of the United States, and Mr. Kalinin of the Supreme Soviet. He asked Roosevelt, the only head of state present, to reply.

Roosevelt answered with a memory from the summer of 1933, his first year as President. His wife had gone to open a school in the country. On its wall hung a map with a great blank space, a place the teacher said it was forbidden to name. The anecdote — about the unrecognized Soviet Union — set the evening's warm tone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d57:
Field Marshal H. Maitland Wilson, head of the British Joint Staff Mission in Washington, wrote to Admiral William Leahy on June 12, 1945. The letter is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Wilson picks up Leahy's suggestion that the two sides swap ideas on an agenda for their military chiefs.

The British Chiefs of Staff, Wilson reports, agree and go further. They want a formal meeting of the Combined Chiefs of Staff tied to the Big Three gathering, held in London beforehand, with three or four clear days for work. The British chiefs will attend the Berlin meeting with small staffs. The main topic, Wilson says, will be the war against Japan, including whether Russia joins it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d157:
Acting Secretary Grew recorded another extract of his June 16, 1945 talk with President Truman. The extract is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, drawn from the same White House meeting that produced document 70. This passage turns to China and the Yalta Far East agreement.

Ambassador Hurley had passed on questions from Chiang Kai-shek about how points in the Yalta agreement would be carried out. Grew told the President he saw no way to answer until the matter had been discussed with Stalin, so replies must wait for the Big Three meeting. Nor could China's Dr. Soong well take the questions up with Stalin alone. The President definitely concurred. The passage shows the Yalta Far East bargain hanging over relations with China.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d257:
A briefing paper documented the shut-out of American reporters in Eastern Europe, dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 257 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It supports the agenda item on freedom of communication and information in Europe.

American correspondents have found it practically impossible even to enter the lands freed by the Soviet armies, the paper says. Soviet military authorities and the Soviet-run control commissions have followed a steady policy of exclusion, and applications since December have been refused or ignored. In Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia the picture is only a little better, with strict censorship. Meanwhile Soviet newsmen enjoy the same freedom in the West that American and British reporters do. The paper lays out the record Washington meant to lay before Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d357:
France's exclusion from the reparations talks fills an extract of Grew's memorandum of a June 25, 1945 conversation with Ambassador Bonnet. The French ambassador came to ask a favor. His government wanted the American ambassador in Moscow told to keep the French ambassador there informed of the three-power Reparations Commission's work.

Bonnet stressed France's deep interest in reparations, and its feeling that a French member should have sat on the Commission. France, he said, had suffered greatly in the war. Grew replied that he would give the request prompt consideration. The extract catches France pressing at the door of a club of three.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d457:
Numbers for the Soviet buildup in Bulgaria follow in Kirk's cable of June 30, 1945, again reporting General Oxley. boucher-antiquites-tome-2-1857:
Jacques Boucher de Perthes was a French customs man and a keen digger. His Antiquities celtiques et antediluviennes, Book Two, came out in French in 1857. The work deals with Celtic and pre-flood finds from the Somme gravel beds. Book One stands just past in the set.

Stone tools found with the bones of lost beasts fill his proof. Boucher held that men lived far past the age the books then gave them. Most sages of his day scoffed, then came round to his side. The set is a root work in the tale of man's deep past.
bronte-the-professor-1857:
Charlotte Brontë wrote The Professor first, and it saw print only in 1857, after her death. The posthumous novel is the seedbed of both Villette and Jane Eyre in her work. Publishers had turned it down nine times while she lived and sought a better fate.

William Crimsworth, a mill owner's son, quits trade and teaches at a Brussels boys' school. He loves Frances Henri, a lace mender and pupil-teacher of Swiss and English blood in Brussels. Jealous heads and a spying director test their modest courtship of work and study there. The pair wed, teach, and prosper in a close, unsentimental close of quiet industry. The plain style shows Brontë before the fire of Jane Eyre lit her prose.
gaskell-life-of-charlotte-bronte-1857:
Elizabeth Gaskell published The Life of Charlotte Brontë in 1857, two years after Brontë's death. Charlotte's father and husband asked Gaskell, her friend, to write the authorized life of her. The book fixed the Brontë myth of the lonely moorland parsonage for the next century.

Gaskell traces Haworth's graves, the sisters' childhood worlds, and their secret writing lives in detail. She tells of Brussels, the Bell books, fame, and the deaths that emptied the house. Some portraits of living people drew threats of lawsuits and forced cuts in later editions printed. Her warm, novelistic hand made the life read like one of Brontë's own tales of Yorkshire. It remains the source all later Brontë lives must start from and argue with.
dumas-companions-of-jehu-1857:
Alexandre Dumas published The Companions of Jehu in 1857, a romance of the French Directory years. The tale follows the royalist Companions of Jehu, highwaymen who robbed state gold for their cause. Secret societies, duels, and Napoleon's rise frame this late and vigorous Dumas historical romance in France.

Roland de Montrevel, a dashing aide to Bonaparte, hunts the Companions across the wild Bresse country. Their chief, Morgan, proves to be Roland's own friend and his sister's secret husband in hiding. Stagecoach raids fund a royalist rising while Bonaparte crushes foes in Italy and Egypt abroad then. The guillotine and the battlefield thin both camps as the Consulate dawns on France victorious. Dumas keeps sympathy divided, a mark of his mature and fairer historical art.
trollope-barchester-towers-1857:
Anthony Trollope published Barchester Towers in 1857, the battle for Barchester's soul in comic form supreme. Mrs. Proudie and Archdeacon Grantly fight for the diocese in a tale many call Victorian comedy's peak. The sequel to The Warden outsold it at once and fixed Trollope's name with the reading public of England.

A new bishop, Dr. Proudie, arrives ruled by his wife and her chaplain, the oily Mr. Slope. Slope schemes for power and for the widowed Eleanor Bold, Harding's daughter, as preferment and love intertwine in Barchester. The Thornes' fête, the Stanhope family's Italian ease, and a score of clerical feuds fill the bustling canvas here. Eleanor finds happiness with the shy Arabin, and Slope is sent packing to London in disgrace at last. Trollope's ease with fools, knaves, and saints makes the cathedral town feel entirely real.
baudelaire-flowers-of-evil-1857:
Charles Baudelaire published The Flowers of Evil in 1857, his condemned masterpiece of spleen and ideal in verse. Many call the book the birth certificate of modern poetry in the judgment of poets since its trial. Baudelaire was fined and six poems banned for offenses against public morals in the Paris of 1857.

The poems move between Spleen, the city's rot and ennui, and Ideal, the reach for beauty beyond it. Lesbos, carrion, wine, and the voyage fill sections that map a soul at war with time and flesh. Baudelaire's form is classical and strict while his matter is modern, urban, and deliberately shocking to bourgeois taste. The banned poems and the trial made the book a banner for art's freedom ever since in France. Every modern poet, from Rimbaud to Eliot, works in a world this book remade.
hegel-philosophy-history-sibree-1857:
G. W. F. Hegel gave his Lectures on the Philosophy of History in Berlin in the 1820s. The English text here is J. Sibree's translation of 1857. Hegel argues that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. Each great people, from China to the German world, plays its part and passes.

He divides history into Oriental, Greek, Roman, and German worlds. Reason, he claims, governs the whole process despite war and suffering. The state is the main carrier of freedom in his account. These lectures seeded Marxism and all later philosophy of history. They remain grand, bold, and hotly debated.
buckle-civilization-england-vol-1-1857:
Henry Thomas Buckle published History of Civilization in England, Volume 1, in 1857. Buckle aimed to make history a science governed by laws. Climate, food, soil, and scenery, he argues, shape the character of nations. Statistics, he claims, show regular patterns even in crime and marriage.

The volume surveys France, Spain, Germany, and Scotland before turning to England. Buckle praises intellect and doubts the power of rulers and churches to drive progress. The book was a sensation and drew fierce attacks. Its positivist program now looks overbold. Yet it changed how Victorians thought history could be written. Volume 2 never matched the first's impact.
tauler-sermons-winkworth-1857:
John Tauler was a Dominican preacher in Strasbourg in the fourteenth century, when plague and church strife shook his city. His sermons, in Winkworth's 1857 translation, carry his mystical preaching to English readers. Tauler belonged to the circle later called the Friends of God.

He urges hearers to sink into the ground of the soul, where God speaks beneath all noise and self-will. His sermons treat birthdays of Christ within the heart, patient suffering, and the prayer that needs no words. Luther admired Tauler, and his voice shaped German devotion long after his death. Winkworth's graceful English helped the sermons find that second life.
miller-testimony-rocks-1857:
The Testimony of the Rocks appeared in 1857, a year after Hugh Miller's death. It gathers lectures the Scottish geologist gave on the link between rocks and scripture. Miller was devout, yet he trusted what the stones showed him.

He argues that the fossil record tells a long, ordered history of life. That history, he holds, can sit beside the Bible's account when both are read with care. Miller speaks to church readers who feared geology would kill faith. His calm case made the book a landmark in the science-and-religion debate. The lectures were among the last works he prepared for print.
plos-pone-0003457:
Christopher Vollmers, Satchidananda Panda, and Luciano DiTacchio built a screening tool for body clocks in 2008. Gene silencing screens had sped up many fields of biology. Mammalian circadian rhythms, the daily body clock, had lagged behind. The team set up a faster screen in human U2OS cells.

Their assay uses small RNAs to knock down genes one by one. Cells with broken clocks then stand out for study. The method runs at medium to high throughput. It should speed the hunt for genes that keep daily time. Clock genes affect sleep, mood, and metabolism across the whole body.
plos-pone-0003557:
Arlene E. Dent and co-authors measured malaria protection across ages in Kenya in this 2008 study. Antibodies can slow the growth of Plasmodium falciparum, the main malaria parasite. Children and adults in Kenya face repeated infection from early life. The team linked antibody strength to age and to parasite loads.

They tested how well each person's antibodies inhibited parasite growth. Older subjects generally carried stronger growth-inhibiting activity. Protection from high parasite levels rose with that activity. The age pattern shows vaccine designers the immunity nature builds slowly. Malaria kills most often in young children, before this slow shield can build up over years of bites. Knowing how fast the shield grows helps set the age targets for any new vaccine drive.
plos-pone-0003657:
Francisco M. Camas and Juan F. Poyatos published this systems biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Gene control networks in the bacterium E. coli reuse small wiring patterns called motifs. Why those patterns appear is debated. Some say use shaped them; others favor chance.

The authors offer a new picture of how motifs assemble in these networks. Their account weighs adaptive and neutral routes side by side. The work helps explain why the control system of a well-studied bacterium is built from the parts it has. That is a basic question in how cells evolve.
plos-pone-0003757:
P. J. Nico de Bruyn, Armanda D. S. Bastos, Candice Eadie, and colleagues published this wildlife study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Die-offs of marine mammals from infection are reported more and more often. Most strike males and females, young and old, alike. This event on land broke that pattern.

Adult male subantarctic fur seals died in large numbers while others were spared. The team asked whether alien mice on the island, possible carriers of disease, were the culprits. Their detective work tests a surprising chain from tiny invaders to very large victims.
plos-pone-0003857:
Thierry Poynard, Patrick Ingiliz, Laure Elkrief, and colleagues published this liver study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Liver fibrosis is traditionally staged by biopsy, an imperfect gold standard that cuts tissue. Non-invasive options include stiffness measurement and blood marker panels such as FibroTest. The team compared their accuracy without a perfect reference.

Their methodology judges concordance between markers in a world without a gold standard. It identifies factors linked to disagreement between the tests. The aim is more accurate staging of liver scarring without the needle, for patients who need repeated checks.
plos-pone-0003957:
Laura J. Marinelli, Mariana Piuri, Zuzana Swigoňová, and co-authors presented a phage engineering method in 2008. Sequencing had revealed hundreds of genomes for bacteria and their viruses, called phages. Some bacteria had easy genetic systems, but phages lagged behind. Building mutant phages stayed slow and hard for many labs.

Their PLOS ONE article describes BRED, a method to rebuild phage genomes. It lets users make mutants and mixed recombinant phages directly. Simpler phage engineering speeds studies of what each phage gene does. Those studies support phage therapy work against resistant bacteria. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004057:
David W. Dowdy, Maria C. Lourenço, Solange C. Cavalcante, and co-authors weighed TB testing costs in Brazil in 2008. Growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis in culture is the closest test to a gold standard. Data on its impact in HIV-infected patients were scarce. Resource-limited settings must judge whether culture is worth its cost.

Their PLOS ONE article assessed culture diagnosis for HIV-infected Brazilian adults. It counted both health impact and cost-effectiveness. HIV and TB together strain clinics across Brazil. Evidence for culture helps labs spend limited budgets wisely. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004157:
Ayumi Kishioka and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fear is a strong emotion that helps animals answer real threats. Too much fear, or fear in the wrong place, sits behind many common psychiatric problems. The amygdala, a small brain region, is thought to be central to learning fear.

The team studied auditory fear conditioning, where an animal learns to fear a tone paired with an unpleasant event. Using only a weak version of that event, they describe a novel form of memory for the learned fear. Their work refines what scientists know about how gentle threats can still leave lasting marks.
plos-pone-0004257:
Tal Yarkoni and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reaction time is one of the most widely used measures in experimental psychology. Yet few fMRI studies had used trial-by-trial differences in reaction time as a predictor in their analyses.

Combining several studies, the team asked which brain regions track how fast a person responds on each trial. They report BOLD signal correlates of reaction time variability in both gray and white matter. The white matter result is striking, since that tissue is usually treated as background in brain scans.
plos-pone-0004357:
Marina Marcet-Houben and Toni Gabaldón published this phylogenomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Combining many sequence alignments to reconstruct a single tree of evolutionary relationships is a recurrent topic in phylogenomics. Critics argue that such an approach cannot properly represent the diversity of histories found across a genome.

The authors frame the problem as the tree versus the forest. They use the fungal tree of life and the topological diversity within the yeast phylome. The phylome is the set of all gene trees for a species. Their study measures how much one species tree hides the forest of differing gene trees.
plos-pone-0004457:
Male fruit flies court females with a set dance of moves. Dimitrije Krstic, Werner Boll, and Markus Noll studied how the senses steer that dance in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fruit fly courtship is a classic model for how brains produce complex inborn behavior. Knowing the wiring alone, though, does not explain the behavior.

The team focused on sensory integration, the merging of sight, smell, sound, and touch into one flow of action. A male must track the female's signals moment by moment and adjust his moves. By tracing how those senses feed the courtship network, the study shows how a small brain runs a flexible routine. The lessons reach toward general rules for how nervous systems turn sense data into behavior.
plos-pone-0004557:
Doing good for others might carry a mental health risk, a possibility examined by Takeo Fujiwara in PLOS ONE in 2009. A previous cross-sectional study, a snapshot at one time, had suggested altruistic behaviors were harmful for major depression. Snapshots cannot show which came first, so a prospective look was needed.

Fujiwara followed the question forward in time, asking whether altruistic behavior is associated with the onset of major depression. The data came from the National Survey of Midlife Development in the United States. The study also separated altruistic acts by their content, since helping a stranger and heavy caregiving are different burdens. A careful answer matters for advice given to volunteers and caregivers alike.
plos-pone-0004657:
A ring of smell detectors in the mouse nose draws input from many sources. Renee Cockerham, Adam Puche, and Steven Munger map its wide links inside the smell brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The nose uses more than one smell system to pick up chemical cues. These systems sit in different places, send signals to different targets, and work in different ways.

One system forms the necklace glomeruli, a ring of round processing units at the back of the olfactory bulb. The team describes their mixed sensory input and their wide links within the bulb. Mixed input plus rich links suggest the ring blends several kinds of smell signals rather than passing on a single channel. That may be how social scent cues are joined with other smells.
plos-pone-0004757:
Elad Maor, Antoni Ivorra, and Boris Rubinsky tested a non heat electric method to remove artery wall muscle cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The method uses strong electric pulses that damage only the cell membrane. All other tissue parts are spared, which sets it apart from heat based removal used in surgery today.

Past work in rodents showed it can reduce excess wall growth after artery injury. The team focused on vessel wall muscle cells, the cells that drive that regrowth. Selective removal could keep treated arteries open longer. It offers a new tool for vascular care.
gosse-omphalos-1857:
Philip Henry Gosse tries to untie the knot of Genesis and geology in Omphalos, from 1857. God, he argues, created the world with the look of age upon it. Fossils lie in the rocks as Adam bore a navel, signs of a past that never truly happened in his bold and strange solution.

Geologists and clergy alike rejected the clever argument at once. The book appeared just as Darwin's Origin loomed over the age. Ingenious yet untestable, it convinced almost no one on either side. It stands as the most famous failed peace treaty between Genesis and geology, a landmark of creationist thought in the Victorian age.
brown-estimate-manners-principles-1757:
Brown's Estimate of the Manners and Principles of the Times, published in 1757, was the most talked-of book of its year in England. Britain had just suffered shocks in the war with France, and readers were ready for a harsh diagnosis. Brown, already known as a controversial clergyman-writer, gave them one.

He charged that England had sunk into luxury, selfishness, and fading religion, and that its ruling class had grown soft. Against that decay he set discipline, public spirit, and a return to serious principle. The book sold by the thousand and provoked answers, sequels, and parodies. It stands as the classic jeremiad of its century, an insider's scolding that tells historians exactly what anxious Britons feared about themselves in the 1750s.
cia-0000009857:
A cave on the Houei Vong, where American pilots were held, is located relative to Ban Kang Muong in an April 1967 item. Ban Kang Muong sits in the Laotian panhandle, near trail country. Caves in the limestone hills served the war as depots, shelters, and cells.

Locating a prison cave by its nearest village gave airmen and planners a usable point. Such sites were nearly invisible from the air and hard to reach on foot. The men inside lived cut off in a way few camp prisoners were. This item fixes one cave prison on the map of Laos's hidden war.
cia-0000012257:
Some files hold secrets; others hold the paperwork that organized them day by day. An undated CIA document, its publication year estimated as 1960, lists titles of articles together with the report numbers of a numbered series of issues. Nothing in the sheet explains the pieces it names.

The list names pieces rather than printing them, so its value lies in what it maps. It shows how the agency catalogued its own reporting, issue by issue and title by title. For readers, the fragment is a reminder that intelligence files contain the plain indexes and inventories of a working bureaucracy.
cia-0000015257: Argentine authorities reported a satellite down in Bolivia, in a CIA file dated April 1, 1978. A fallen object near a border set off checks on both sides. Space junk and lost craft fell often in those years. The file holds the first word on a fall that later reports would sort out.
cia-0000022157: Survivors of a C-46 crash were in apparent good condition, and Pathet Lao plans for them are covered in a CIA record dated in 1963. The C-46 was a large transport plane of older design. A crash in Laos left its crew in the hands of the Pathet Lao. Good condition was rare good news in a file full of loss.
cia-0000022357: TASS said Powers could face death, and his case was referred to the Russian Supreme Court, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. TASS was the Soviet state news agency, speaking with official weight. A death threat raised the stakes before the trial even opened. The referral note shows the case moving through the highest Soviet court channels that summer.
cia-0000036557: Photo comparisons for MIA and POW cases 10,147 through 10,158 are the subject of a CIA record dated February 3, 1969, and the case names are blank in the released copy. Analysts compared photographs side by side, hunting for a match that could name a prisoner. A numbered batch like this one shows how large the caseload had grown, and each case stood for a family waiting on an answer.
cia-0000037157:
The burial site of an American military officer near Hong Ho, in Binh Tri Thien province, fills a CIA record dated June 1, 1963. The date is early: American advisers, not armies, were then serving in Vietnam. An officer's grave in 1963 belongs to the war's small and quiet beginning.

The record marks where the officer was said to be buried. Early losses like this one were few enough that each grave was noted on its own. The file shows that the careful accounting of American dead in Vietnam began long before the big battles, with single names and single graves in far provinces.
cia-0000045257:
A prisoner tied to the Duarte kidnapping was pardoned, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A pardon is a formal act of mercy by the state. In a kidnapping case, mercy is rarely separate from bargaining.

Inside, the clemency granted to the prisoner is placed on record. Pardons in such cases are usually part of a larger quiet deal. They free one person as the price of freeing another person. The law's clean language of pardon hid a trade that everyone involved understood at once. The file holds that price in its official form, a legal act on paper that carried, behind it, the whole weight of the crisis.
cia-0000049057: An allegation by the chief of ARENA, El Salvador's hard-right party, fills a CIA item from 1983. The charge touches the paramilitary world that surrounded the party in the war years. ARENA's words and the death squads' deeds were the two halves of the right that Washington had to judge.
cia-0000049257:
The FMLN after its November 1989 offensive is sized up in a CIA paper from 1990, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. The offensive had carried guerrilla fighters into the capital's wealthiest neighborhoods and proved the war could not be won by either side. The paper asks what the front looked like after its greatest effort.

Inside, the movement is weighed after battle: its strength spent or saved, its politics hardened or softened, its appetite for talks. The answers mattered because the war's endgame began with that offensive, at the negotiating table it forced into being. The paper catches the rebels at the turn from war toward peace.
cia-0000049357: Investigations into the murders of six U.S. citizens and a disappearance are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049357, dated September 5, 1982. The heading, cut short in the catalog, frames the file around official inquiries. Readers find a dated agency item about those investigations, kept as a brief record rather than a full account of the cases themselves.
cia-0000075857: Monitoring the Biological and Toxin Weapons Convention is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075857, dated February 1, 1991, subtitled Looking for a Needle in a Haystack. The paper frames treaty monitoring as a hard search problem. Its vivid subtitle is the record's most memorable feature, preserved in a short declassified item on weapons treaty oversight.
cia-0000096657: Current Developments in Chinese Communist Agriculture, with Chinese misspelled in the heading, is declassified CIA document 0000096657, dated July 4, 1968. The title promises a farm-sector update from China. Readers find a short declassified agriculture paper whose spelling flaw is preserved in the catalog, a companion in subject to the earlier rice crop report.

arxiv-2606-14957: Made public on arXiv in 2026, this research paper details a new study. The paper's title identifies its subject: Learning Sparse Latent Predictive Foundation Model for Multimodal Neuroimaging. The subject area is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. The research reported here is now part of the open record.
arxiv-2606-15057: Released to arXiv in 2026, this paper contributes a new study. The title's topic is AutoDojo: Adaptive Black-Box Attacks Reveal the Limits of IPI Defenses and Task-Specification Effects .... It contributes to artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. Its pages carry fresh research aimed at the field's practitioners.
arxiv-2606-15157: Among 2026 arXiv preprints, this manuscript stands as a new research report. Its title gives the subject as PolyKV: Heterogeneous Retention and Allocation for KV Cache Compression. Its discipline is computer science: how computers, software, and data systems are designed and built. Fresh scholarship fills these pages.
arxiv-2606-15357: A 2026 scientific preprint on arXiv, this manuscript documents new work. The title's topic is Fast genomic read alignment with minibwa. The field in play is artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. It contributes fresh work that later studies can cite and extend.
arxiv-2606-15457: A 2026 preprint from arXiv, this paper presents original research. Readers can expect the paper to address Lesion-DDPM: Lesion-Enhanced 3D Diffusion for MS MRI Synthesis. The work sits within artificial intelligence — the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. The work reported here becomes part of the open literature.
plos-pone-0004857:
Barkha Srivastava and colleagues showed host genetic background strongly influences response to influenza A infections, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genetic makeup of the host has major influence on combating pathogens. For influenza A, several single gene mutations contribute to survival, immune response, and clearance. The team compared genetically distinct mouse lines challenged with virus to quantify background effects on disease.

Some backgrounds resist while others succumb quickly. Mouse choice therefore shapes experimental conclusions. Human diversity likely mirrors that range. Personalized risk prediction may follow genetic mapping. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0005457:
Eric Sijbrands, Erik Tornij, and Sietske Homsma followed a huge group of men for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Insurance firms use medical checks to judge how long an applicant is likely to live. People now debate whether gene tests should be added to those checks.

The authors compared what one firm predicted for tens of thousands of men with what really happened over time. Knowing how well the old method works sets a fair bar for any new gene-based method. The long follow-up gives rare hard evidence in a debate often run on guesses.
plos-pone-0005557:
Abdelali Agouni and co-authors tested red wine compounds in obese rats for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Obesity raises the risk of heart and blood vessel disease. Population studies link plant compounds called flavonoids, found in foods such as grapes, with lower death rates from heart disease.

The team fed compounds from red wine to a strain of rats bred to become fat. They checked the rats' metabolism and blood vessel health for signs of protection. Early animal results like these guide, but cannot prove, dietary advice for people. Fatty rats are a standard first test, but human trials would be needed before any claim could be made for people.
plos-pone-0005657:
Daniel Correia and co-authors studied signals in anti-tumour T cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A special group of T cells reacts to small phosphate compounds from microbes. That reaction is the basis of efforts to use these cells against cancer.

A highly active microbial compound switched the cells on fast and kept two signalling paths running for a long time. Strong, lasting signals may explain the cells' strong anti-tumour action. Knowing the paths helps design treatments that wake these cells up in patients. Cancer use of these cells is still early, and mapping their signals is basic groundwork for any trial.
plos-pone-0005757:
Lichuan Yang and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a synthetic compound can shield nerve cells by switching on their defense genes. The switch, Nrf2, turns on a battery of detox and antioxidant enzymes. The compound, CDDO methyl amide, is a potent activator of that switch.

In their tests, the compound showed neuroprotective effects worth pursuing for brain diseases. Many such diseases involve oxidative stress that Nrf2 defenses counter. A drug that safely raises those defenses could help across several conditions. The study adds evidence for the approach and details the compound's action in nerve tissue.
plos-pone-0005857:
W. Shawn Carbonell and co-authors challenged in 2009 the standard picture of how cancer spreads to the brain. The classic seed-and-soil idea holds that tumor cells seek out brain tissue itself, drawn by its special chemistry. Direct evidence for that neurotropic growth in living animals was thin.

Instead, the team found metastases growing along the vascular basement membrane, the sleeve around brain blood vessels. The vessel wall, not the neurons, may be the true soil. That shift in view changes where researchers look for the signals that feed brain metastases. It may suggest blocking the vessel niche to starve them.
plos-pone-0006457:
Maria Morales and Robert Gereau checked a routine lab practice in PLOS ONE in 2009. To genotype mice, staff often snip a small piece of tail at weaning and take DNA from it. That is how genetically modified mice are identified. But when such mice are used in pain research, the snip itself could alter how the animals respond to painful stimuli.

The authors tested whether tail biopsy changes behavioral responses to noxious stimuli. A practice meant only to label animals might quietly bias pain data. Their study warns pain researchers to account for the procedure. It also speaks to animal welfare, since a common step may carry lasting effects.
plos-pone-0006557:
Elodie Fino, Jean-Michel Deniau, and Laurent Venance showed small signals can drive lasting brain change in PLOS ONE in 2009. Action potentials are thought to be determinant for inducing long-term synaptic plasticity. That plasticity is the cellular basis of learning and memory. However, neuronal activity does not always reach full spikes.

The authors show brief subthreshold events can act as Hebbian signals for long-term plasticity. Hebbian learning strengthens connections when cells are active together. If small, below-threshold events count, learning rules are more forgiving than thought. The finding reshapes models of how synapses decide to change.
plos-pone-0009457:
Jie Zhu and colleagues traced the history of a hormone part in PLOS ONE in 2010. Inhibin is a hormone that puts a brake on signals tied to reproduction. It belongs to the large TGF beta family of signal proteins. Its alpha part is found in no close cousin, which makes it stand out. The team searched genomes across animal groups.

By comparing those genomes, they worked out when the alpha part first arose. Their tree shows how a new piece could join an old family and gain a fresh role. The study explains the birth of a one of a kind brake in animal reproduction. It also shows how gene families grow by invention.
plos-pone-0009557:
Wei-Guo Du, Bo Zhao, and Richard Shine tracked turtle heart rates around hatching in PLOS ONE in 2010. Turtles are cold blooded, so heat speeds their hearts. Embryos gain from fast growth, since a shorter stay in the egg means less risk. Speed costs energy, though. The team measured heart rates of embryos and hatchlings at high temperatures.

Embryos kept high heart rates when warm. After hatching, the same high temperatures no longer drove the heart as fast. So the animal retunes its heart for its new life stage. The change balances the need for speed in the egg against safety outside it.
plos-pone-0009657:
Yosef Buganim and co-authors found a chromosome break tied to early cancer change in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sometimes two chromosomes swap pieces, and the break point lands inside a gene. Here the break falls inside BPTF, a gene that helps control how DNA is packaged and read. Cells carrying the break showed a pre malignant character. The team characterized the break and those cell traits.

A pre malignant state is a step on the road to cancer, not cancer itself. Catching such steps clarifies how malignancy begins. The break in BPTF may disturb gene control enough to prime cells for later change. Studies of this kind help map the earliest events that screening might one day detect.
plos-pone-0010457:
Andrea Petróczi and colleagues questioned whether athletes who deny doping can be believed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on doping leans heavily on athletes' own reports. Studies of drug use show people under-report stigmatized behavior. Doping is both banned and shamed, so under-reporting is likely worse. The authors looked behind clean self-reports for signs of pretense.

They explored indirect ways to detect hidden doping attitudes and use. Better measurement matters because policy built on false low numbers will fail. The study treats honesty itself as the variable to test. That is a brave move in a field built on questionnaires. Its lessons apply to any survey of forbidden behavior.
plos-pone-0010557:
Manuel Forero and colleagues released an automatic counter for dividing cells and glial cells in fly tissues in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell counts change in growth, degeneration, and cancer. Genetic studies therefore often need counts after a gene is lost or boosted. Counting cells by eye in images is slow and error-prone. Their tool, DeadEasy Mito-Glia, counts the two cell types in fruit fly images automatically.

Automation makes large genetic screens with cell counts practical. Consistent machine counts also remove human drift between scorers. The fly is a workhorse for gene function studies, so the audience is large. Tools like this quietly change what experiments are feasible. The paper documents accuracy as well as speed.
plos-pone-0010657:
Hridayesh Prakash and colleagues studied a fat-based signal that helps immune cells fight germs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The cells are called macrophages, and they swallow germs that enter the body. An enzyme inside them, sphingosine kinase-1, makes the signal when a fight starts.

The team exposed mouse macrophages to Mycobacterium smegmatis, a kin of the TB germ. When the enzyme was blocked, the cells held far fewer germs in check. When it worked as usual, the cells kept the germs down. Boosting a host defense like this might aid TB drugs one day, with less risk of drug failure.
plos-pone-0010757:
Camila Figueiredo Pinzan and colleagues asked why one fungal disease strikes men far more than women, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Paracoccidioidomycosis is a whole-body fungal infection found across Latin America. At least ten men fall ill for every woman, a gap too large for exposure alone to explain.

Male and female mice were infected under matched conditions. Their immune responses diverged clearly, with females mounting the stronger defense. Hormones and immune wiring both seemed to play a part. Sex gaps this wide hint that treatments and vaccine plans may need to account for sex, not treat it as noise.
plos-pone-0010857:
Sean Carlin, Nahida Khan, Thomas Ku and co-authors published this imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many tumors contain low-oxygen zones that resist treatment, and a protein called CAIX helps those zones manage acid. The authors tested whether an antibody aimed at CAIX could find such zones in living tumors.

They compared a full antibody and two smaller fragments, each tagged so its path could be tracked, in mice carrying human colon tumors. The tumors showed strong CAIX in poorly supplied, low-oxygen areas, and the agents gathered there in different patterns. The full antibody first lit up the rim of those zones. Carlin and colleagues weigh which form best reports tumor hypoxia. A reliable hypoxia tracer could help doctors pick patients for oxygen-targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0010957:
Matthew Becker and Reid Harris published this salamander study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The chytrid fungus devastating amphibians worldwide grows on skin, and earlier lab work showed that bacteria living on redback salamander skin can inhibit it. The authors tested whether that skin community actually protects living salamanders from the disease.

They reduced the skin bacteria of some salamanders before exposing them to the fungus, and compared them with infected salamanders keeping a normal community. The reduced-bacteria animals lost significantly more body mass, a disease symptom, and more of them showed limb loss. Becker and Harris demonstrate that a salamander's resident microbes act as a living shield. That finding supports probiotic-style treatments being explored to save threatened frog populations.
plos-pone-0011057:
Teiichiro Shiino, Nobuhiko Okabe, Yoshinori Yasui and co-authors published this flu evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 pandemic H1N1 virus reached Japan in May of that year, sparking outbreaks in Osaka and Hyogo before spreading across prefectures. The authors reconstructed the virus's family tree from full genomes to trace how it entered and moved through the country.

Comparing dozens of Japanese isolates with worldwide sequences, using both distance and Bayesian statistical methods, they found the global viruses fell into four distinct clusters. One cluster arose earlier, while another spread most widely around the world. Shiino and colleagues show the Japanese epidemic drew from that global structure rather than a single introduction. Such profiles help public health officials distinguish imported cases from homegrown transmission chains.
plos-pone-0011157:
Dusa, Mouton, Pecquet and colleagues pinpointed a blood cancer target in PLOS ONE in 2010. A mutant form of a signaling protein stays switched on and drives some blood cancers. The mutant needs help from a second region of the same protein to stay active, and the team located a key spot in that region.

That spot, a single building block in a helper domain, proved required for constant activity. A drug aimed there could block the mutant while sparing normal signaling proteins. Such precise blockers promise fewer side effects than broad drugs. The finding turns a structural detail into a concrete drug design goal.
plos-pone-0011257:
Klassen compared pigment genes across microbes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria make carotenoids, the bright pigments that color carrots and autumn leaves. By comparing pigment making genes across many genomes, the author traced how this pathway evolved and spread among microbes.

The patterns show the recipe was inherited, borrowed and reshaped over long time spans. Knowing its history helps industry find microbes that make useful pigments. Those pigments serve as vitamins, food colors and health products. Evolution thus becomes a prospecting guide for biotechnology, pointing to lineages most likely to yield new products.
plos-pone-0011357:
Yurong Xin and colleagues compared DNA marks across two major brain regions in a 2010 study. Cells add chemical tags to DNA that help set which genes stay active, and the pattern differs from tissue to tissue. The team mapped those tags genome-wide in the cerebrum, the seat of thought, and the cerebellum, which fine-tunes movement.

The two regions carried clearly divergent tag patterns, far more distinct than a simple tissue label would predict. Many differences fell near genes with brain roles, hinting that tagging helps lock in each region's identity. The maps give neuroscientists a baseline for spotting tag changes in brain disease. They also show that studies pooling the whole brain can hide strong regional contrasts that matter for how the brain works.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1257:
Togo wrote to Sato on 27 July 1945, the day after the Potsdam Declaration reached Tokyo. The Allied terms demanded surrender and left the throne's fate unclear. Japan's leaders split over the answer, and Togo, who sought an end, kept his Moscow channel alive.

His instruction to Sato shows the foreign minister still working the Soviet door as the crisis peaked. If Moscow would mediate, Tokyo might gain terms the declaration denied it. That hope, thin as Sato's reports had shown it to be, drove this cable. It is Tokyo's hand on its last lever, pulled on the declaration's morrow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1357:
Secretary of State James Byrnes wrote to the acting secretary of state on 23 July 1945, reporting from the Potsdam side of the Atlantic. The channel between Byrnes and Grew ran in both directions all through the conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Most papers in this run flow from Washington toward the summit, so a message from Byrnes homeward stands out. The secretary abroad still had to steer his own department: staff, budgets, and other talks all needed his hand. Readers get a sense of the two-way strain of summit diplomacy. The man at the table must also run the office he left behind in Washington.
frus-1945-50-intel-d57:
Admiral Chester Nimitz, now chief of naval operations, wrote to Secretary Forrestal on 15 December 1945. Nimitz had taken over the Navy's top uniformed post the month before. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Nimitz brought the prestige of the Pacific victory to every paper he signed. His views on intelligence, formed in a theater where code-breaking had won battles, carried weight beyond their words. Readers should note the change of hand: King had guarded the Navy's claims through the autumn; Nimitz now held them as the settlement neared. The Navy's thread in the volume thus passes from one great wartime admiral to another without losing its force.
frus-1945-50-intel-d157:
A memorandum dated 21 June 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was C. H. Carson of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The reader was the Assistant Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Ladd). It is document 157 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d257:
On 17 December 1947, the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 257 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The ink on the National Security Act was barely dry, and both the CIA and the Council were finding their feet.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d357:
The Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum) addressed a letter to Mathias F. Correa on 18 December 1948. Readers meet it as document 357 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The letter form mattered in this world: it was signed, it was kept, and it bound the writer's office to what it said. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1861-d57:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 June 1861. It is document 57 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

As June closed, both American armies moved toward their first great clash. Adams could only report London's talk and wait, like Seward, for news. His letter shows an envoy holding his post steady while events at home rushed toward battle. From London, even the clash of armies came first as rumor, then as dread fact. Rumor in London ran fast, and Adams learned to sift it with a cold eye.
frus-1861-d157:
A round of letters on 21 October 1861 included one from William H. Seward to William Dayton. The letter is document 157 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Paris and to Berlin in the same late October round. The letters kept each post aware that it formed part of one front. Dayton's copy shows the Secretary's hand at work across the map in a single week. The round of late October letters spans the map of the Union's foreign front. One week, one hand, a whole front: the round shows the office at its peak load.
frus-1861-d257:
Washington's orders went out to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands in a dispatch dated 4 October 1861. Congress received it as Document 257 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d57:
A dispatch dated 2 May 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 57 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d157:
Secretary of State William H. Seward directed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams in London on 4 October 1862, printed as Document 157 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams, the American minister to Britain, acted on these orders in his talks with British officials.

Orders from Washington had to cover events the Secretary could not foresee, since replies took weeks. Seward therefore mixed firm lines with room for his envoy's judgment. A letter from this week belongs to the stretch when Britain, after Antietam. Chose to wait rather than step into the war, a choice Adams worked to make permanent.
frus-1862-d257:
Dated 8 March 1862, Document 257 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

The day after Seward wrote, the ironclad Virginia attacked Union ships at Hampton Roads, and the Monitor fought it to a draw. Naval news like that echoed loudly in France, a great sea power with its own ironclad plans. Seward's letters to Paris in March belonged to a season when each battle reset foreign guesses about the war. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d357:
On 10 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Henri Mercier another letter, printed as Document 357 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Mercier was the French minister in Washington throughout this period.

Two letters in four days show the French channel carrying steady traffic in the winter of 1862. Much of that traffic was case work: ships, trade, and the rights of French citizens caught by the war. Such business rarely made headlines, but it filled the envoys' days and kept the larger relationship in repair. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English.
frus-1862-d457:
John Lothrop Motley wrote from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 February 1862. His report is Document 457 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

February 1862 brought a run of Union victories, and Motley's reports could carry that improving story into Austrian ears. Still, Vienna moved slowly and spoke carefully, and its press often echoed Confederate hopes. A minister's dispatch in such a place was part news, part weather report on opinion. Seward gathered these readings from every capital before deciding where the dangers lay. Motley's February letter is one gauge in that wider instrument panel.
frus-1862-d557:
A Mr. Goodrich received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1862. It is Document 557 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed among the Belgian papers of that summer.

The letter sits in the file between Seward's orders to Minister Sanford in Brussels, part of the same run of Belgian business. Instructions of this kind carried Washington's directions to the officers who served the mission and its work. July 1862 was a month of strain, with the Virginia campaign gone wrong, and every post abroad needed steady direction. The document is a reminder that a legation was a small team. The State Department's paper reached beyond the minister whose name heads the file.
frus-1862-d657:
On 9 December 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Robert H. Pruyn, who was set to lead the American legation in Japan. The letter is document 657 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Townsend Harris, the first minister to Japan, was on his way out of the post.

Before an envoy sailed, the State Department loaded him with written orders. Seward's letters to Pruyn that winter formed the base of the new man's charge. This letter is one of them. It shows how much care Washington took with a post that guarded trade and the flag in a land still new to American ships.
frus-1863p1-d57: A Mr. St. John wrote this letter to a Mr. Smith on 28 October 1862. It is document 57 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the last of the Confederate group printed there. The evidence names the two men and the date, but not their posts or the letter's subject. This note stays within those bounds.
frus-1863p1-d157:
On 16 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 157 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Adams's pair took the next head of the London news in line. That April, the news ran from the shipyards to Parliament, and the legation sorted it all for home. This letter is the mate to document 156. With it, the pair shows the post's mid-April pace: steady, split by topic, and aimed at a reader who used every page.
frus-1863p1-d257:
An instruction dated 7 August 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 257 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Union victories in July 1863 let Washington speak with more confidence. Orders sent after Gettysburg and Vicksburg carry a firmer note than those of the spring. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d357:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 10 January 1863. It appears as document 357 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d457:
A letter of 11 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 457 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d557:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State took up his pen on 8 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d657:
Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 6 November 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the late autumn of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
plos-pbio-0020057:
David Serre, André Langaney, Mario Chech, and a large team tested ancient DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. They pulled mitochondrial DNA, the small genome passed down by mothers, from Neandertal fossils and from early modern human fossils. The question was whether Neandertals left genes in people alive today.

Mitochondrial DNA from the early modern humans matched living people, while the Neandertal type stayed apart. The authors found no sign that Neandertal maternal lines survived into our species. That result shaped debate on how modern humans spread out of Africa. It suggested replacement more than mixing, at least along the maternal line that this kind of DNA can trace.
plos-pbio-0020257:
Marina Kniazeva, Quinn T. Crawford, Matt Seibel, and their team found a fat the worm C. elegans cannot live without, reported in PLOS Biology in 2004. The fat is a branched-chain fatty acid with a single branch. This tiny worm is a standard lab animal for studying growth.

Without this fat, worm embryos fail to develop properly. A fat acting as an essential building signal is more than fuel; it is part of the growth program itself. The study gives the worm field a new required nutrient to track. It also hints that branched fats, long ignored next to common fats, may hold key roles in other animals too.
plos-pone-0000157:
Angèle Viola, Véronique Saywell, Laurent Villard, and colleagues published this brain chemistry study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It uses a mouse model of Rett syndrome, a disorder that disrupts brain development, mostly in girls. The authors built metabolic fingerprints of the model, profiling chemical changes tied to brain growth, water balance, and neurotransmission.

A fingerprint of small-molecule changes can reveal what a gene defect does to the brain in practice. The authors map those shifts across the systems named in the title. Such profiles help researchers judge disease severity and test whether a treatment moves the brain's chemistry back toward normal.
plos-pone-0000257:
Antoinette C. van der Kuyl, Remco van den Burg, Fokla Zorgdrager, and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Sialoadhesin, also called CD169, is a protein on the surface of certain immune cells, the CD14+ cells tracked here. The authors report that its expression rises early after HIV-1 infection and keeps increasing as the disease progresses.

A protein that climbs steadily from early infection onward is a candidate marker of disease stage. The authors measure that climb in patients over time. The work also raises questions about what this adhesion protein does for, or against, the virus as infection advances.
plos-pone-0000357:
Caroline Costedoat, Nicolas Pech, Rémi Chappaz, and colleagues published this evolutionary biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hybrid zones are places where two species or populations meet and interbreed. The authors present novelties in hybrid zones, framing them as a crossroads between population genomic and ecological approaches to the same natural laboratories.

Hybrid zones reveal what keeps species apart and what lets genes cross. Combining genomic scans with field ecology gives a fuller account than either alone. The paper argues for that combined approach and illustrates what it can find.
plos-pone-0000457:
Ekaterina Dadachova and colleagues reported that radiation feeds certain fungi instead of only harming them, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Melanin, the dark pigment in these fungi, changes its electronic properties when hit by ionizing radiation. The team found that this change enhances the growth of melanized fungi.

Melanized fungi are famously found in extreme places, including the walls of the damaged Chernobyl reactor. A pigment that converts radiation into usable energy would explain that success, making melanin act a little like chlorophyll does for light. The work suggests radiation is not a universal poison but, for the right chemistry, a resource.
plos-pone-0000557:
Simone S. Santos-Lopes, Rinaldo W. Pereira, and Ian J. Wilson traced the human X chromosome's history across the world, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A phylogeography reconstructs where lineages lived and how they spread. Their worldwide phylogeography for the human X chromosome used its inheritance pattern, two copies in women and one in men, to read population history.

The X chromosome records male and female histories differently, so it can reveal sex-biased migrations that other markers miss.
