Comparing its tree with those from the Y chromosome and mitochondria gives a fuller account of how peoples moved. Such studies underlie much of what genetics says about human origins.
plos-pone-0000657:
Cornelia Thedieck, Hubert Kalbacher, Markus Kuczyk and co-authors announced a new surface marker for kidney fibroblasts in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fibroblasts in the kidney's interstitial tissue are a minor share of its cells but a very important one. They secrete and remodel the matrix around cells and produce active compounds such as erythropoietin, the hormone that drives red blood cell production.

Studying human renal fibroblasts had been hampered by a lack of suitable markers to identify them. The title names cadherin-9 as that marker for this mixed cell pool. A reliable tag lets researchers pull these cells out of tissue and study kidney scarring directly.
plos-pone-0000757:
Pieter W. Uys, Robin M. Warren and Paul D. van Helden put a number on how long tuberculosis can wait before diagnosis becomes dangerous. In communities where TB is common, transmission is the major force driving the epidemic. The typically long delay from onset of infectious disease to diagnosis and treatment is plausibly the major factor behind continued spread.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study seeks a threshold value for that delay. Below the threshold, each case infects few enough others that control can hold. Above it, the epidemic feeds itself. A concrete threshold tells clinics how fast is fast enough, turning a vague call for earlier diagnosis into a measurable target.
plos-pone-0000857:
Sittiporn Pattaradilokrat, Sandra J. Cheesman and Richard Carter hunted the genes that make malaria immunity strain-specific. Protection against blood-stage malaria works in part only against the strain a person has met before. The targets of that strain-specific protection should therefore differ between parasite lines, in both their genes and the immune response they raise.

Their method is called linkage group selection. Parasite strains are crossed, and the young that survive strain-specific immunity are checked for which genome chunks they kept. Chunks kept under pressure point to the target genes. Such targets are prime vaccine leads, since natural immunity already proves they can be hit. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000957:
Marielle Gold, Tammie Robinson, Matthew Cook and colleagues showed that newborn dendritic cells can handle a key immune task, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Newborns fall harder to many infections than adults do. The usual explanation is an immature immune system, but several parts of newborn immunity simply differ from the adult form.

Dendritic cells start immune responses by processing antigens and presenting them. The team report that human neonatal dendritic cells are competent at the class I form of that job. A strength in newborns, where weakness was assumed, changes the picture. It may also matter for designing vaccines that work in the first weeks of life.
plos-pone-0001057:
Ian Cowell, Nicola Sunter, Prim Singh and colleagues mapped where a DNA damage mark forms in the genome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. H2A.X is a histone variant making up to a quarter of its family in mammal cells. Within minutes of a DNA double strand break, nearby H2A.X molecules gain a phosphate tag, forming foci that flag the damage.

The team report those foci form preferentially in euchromatin, the open, active parts of the genome. Where damage flags rise fastest may shape how repair proceeds. Open regions hold the genes a cell is using, so fast marking there has clear logic. The map guides repair research.
plos-pone-0001157:
In hybrids, one parent's set of ribosomal RNA genes often falls silent while the other's keeps working, a phenomenon called nucleolar dominance. Olga Pontes and co-authors studied when that silencing is set up, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The silenced region can stretch over megabases of DNA.

The authors describe the postembryonic establishment of this large-scale silencing, meaning it takes shape after the embryo stage rather than being fixed from the start. Ribosomal RNA genes sit in tandem arrays, and choosing between parental copies is an epigenetic decision. Their timing findings clarify how such a sweeping choice gets locked in during development.
plos-pone-0001257:
Epstein-Barr virus persists in its host for life as episomes, small circles of viral DNA kept in the cell nucleus. Jayaraju Dheekollu and colleagues studied how those episomes copy and stay stable, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The virus's origin of plasmid replication, OriP, gives this episomal upkeep.

The authors report roles for the DNA repair proteins MRE11 and NBS1, and for recombination junctions, in copying and keeping the episomes. Structures formed at replication origins may support fidelity and chromosome stability in general. Their findings link how the virus persists to the host's own repair tools.
plos-pone-0001357:
Respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, is a major cause of infant lung infections, and fast diagnosis guides care. Ramona Tillmann and colleagues evaluated a commercial NASBA assay for detecting RSV in clinical specimens, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They compared three diagnostic procedures, including an FDA-cleared ELISA kit and an in-house RT-PCR protocol.

The aim was to judge how usable the three methods are, side by side. NASBA amplifies RNA directly and can be faster than culture-based methods. Hospital labs need a sensitive commercial assay that works well on real samples. This study tested exactly that.
plos-pone-0001457:
Suha Naffar-Abu-Amara and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on genes that help cancer cells move. Cell movement is a complex act steered by many genes and signals. To find genes or drugs that change it, labs need screens that watch movement in fine detail. The team built a screen based on fast, counted microscopy.

With that screen they found new genes that push cancer cells to migrate. Cell spread is what makes many cancers lethal, so each new driver matters. Hits from the screen give drug teams fresh targets to test. The method itself can be reused for other movement based hunts.
plos-pone-0001557:
Yuan-Chang Chao and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on dengue fever and a common enzyme lack. The lack, called G6PD deficiency, is rife in Asia, where dengue is also rife. The team asked whether the lack changes how dengue infects blood cells. They used cells drawn from donors with and without the lack.

Cells from donors with the lack took up more of one dengue type. That hints the lack may raise risk or weight of dengue in those who bear it. In lands where both are common, the link has real public health weight. It urges joint screening where funds allow.
plos-pone-0001657:
Jeri D. Barak and Anita S. Liang traced how Salmonella bacteria reach tomato plants in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tomatoes had become the food most often blamed for produce-linked salmonellosis in the United States, with 12 outbreaks since 1998. Trace-back work pointed to contamination before harvest, in the field, but the routes were unproven.

The authors tested three suspects: the soil, crop debris left in fields, and a plant pathogen that infects tomatoes. The full text gives the greenhouse and field tests and where the bacteria turned up on the plants. Knowing which route matters most tells growers where to act, whether in soil care, debris cleanup, or disease control, to keep a common food safer.
plos-pone-0001757:
Shizhong Han, Joel M. Guthridge, Isaac T. W. Harley, and their co-authors tested a bone protein's gene for links to lupus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Osteopontin, made by the SPP1 gene, is a bone matrix mediator with key roles in inflammation and immunity. Earlier small studies had tied SPP1 variants and high osteopontin levels to systemic lupus erythematosus.

The team evaluated the association in a larger study and report a probable gene-gender interaction: the effect differs between men and women. The full text gives the patient groups and the variant statistics. Sex-dependent gene effects fit lupus, a disease far commoner in women, and they warn that genetic studies pooling sexes can miss real signals.
plos-pone-0001857:
Michael T. Bethune, Erin Ribka, Chaitan Khosla, and their co-authors studied gluten handling in gluten-sensitive macaques in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In previous work the group characterized gluten sensitivity in juvenile rhesus macaques similar in many respects to human celiac disease. The animal model may therefore be useful for studying both how gluten crosses the gut lining and how it can be detoxified.

The team examined transepithelial transport and enzymatic detoxification of gluten in these macaques. The full text gives the transport measurements and the enzyme treatments. Enzyme pills that digest gluten in the stomach are a leading celiac therapy idea. This primate model tests them in a gut much like ours.
plos-pone-0001957:
Christer Bronmark and co-authors asked why fish in lakes migrate with the seasons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Migration is common in land and water animals alike, and much work has gone into why it evolved and what it does to populations. In lakes, fish often move between deep and shallow zones across the year.

As the title states, the team frames the move as a trade-off: shallow water offers faster growth, but also more predators. Fish shift zones as the balance of food and risk changes with the season. Framing migration as a bargain helps predict how lake life will shift when climates or predator numbers change.
plos-pone-0002057:
Olivier Delmas and co-authors read the full genomes of the rabies virus family, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Lyssaviruses are RNA viruses that cause rabies-like diseases in mammals. Past genome and evolution studies had mostly used partial sequences, above all two genes, with little from the rest of the genome.

The team compared complete genomes across the family to chart its genomic diversity and evolution. A fuller tree can show where new rabies-like viruses come from and how they adapt to bats and other hosts. That matters for vaccines, which must cover a moving family.
plos-pone-0002157:
Markus Pfenninger and Carsten Nowak asked how two near-twin midge species manage to live side by side, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The non-biting midges Chironomus riparius and Chironomus piger look almost the same and can breed with each other in the lab. Yet in nature they often share the same waters without merging into one species.

The authors studied the larvae to see how the two split their living space and food, a pattern called niche partition. They also weighed the barriers that keep the species apart. The case offers a clean look at how new species can form while still living in the same place.
plos-pone-0002257:
Langzhou Song, Valerian Nakaar, Uma Kavita, and co-authors made influenza vaccine proteins in bacteria at high yield, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Linking a vaccine antigen to a molecule that alarms the immune system is known to make the vaccine stronger. The team applied that trick to the flu's protective surface protein, hemagglutinin.

They fused the head of hemagglutinin to a bacterial alarm signal and produced the vaccine in bacteria, a fast and cheap factory. High yields from a simple system could ease the chronic shortage of flu vaccine in pandemics and bad seasons alike. Recombinant vaccines like these can be redesigned quickly when the virus changes.
plos-pone-0002357:
Grant Challen and Margaret Goodell examined a fluorescent labeling trick for finding quiet stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Studying adult stem cells depends on isolating them with complex mixes of markers. A recent method used a switchable H2B-GFP mouse: cells that divide rarely keep the glowing tag longest, mimicking classic pulse-chase labeling.

The team reports that the H2B-GFP transgene is expressed promiscuously in hematopoietic stem cells, switched on in cells it should not mark. That leakiness can mislead studies that trust the label. A caution from inside the field helps every lab using the model read its results more carefully.
plos-pone-0002457: Jakob Schnetzer and co-authors published the article in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at the early ANTP gene set through the genome of a placozoan, a very simple sea animal. ANTP genes help guide how an animal body takes shape as it grows. Placozoans sit near the base of animal life, so their genes offer clues about first body plans.
plos-pone-0002557:
Wang and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Xiaohong Wang, Shuang Tang, Shu-Yun Le, among others. Its subject is aberrant Expression of Oncogenic and Tumor-Suppressive MicroRNAs in Cervical Cancer Is Required for Cancer Cell Growth. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play important roles in cancer development.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002657:
Sallouha Aidoudi and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of the CXC-Chemokine CXCL4 interacts with integrins implicated in angiogenesis. Authorship is credited in the record to Sallouha Aidoudi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The human CXC-chemokine CXCL4 is a potent inhibitor of tumor-induced angiogenesis. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002757:
In 2008, E. Alejandro Herrada and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about universal scaling in the branching of the tree of life. The full author list in the catalog record begins with E. Alejandro Herrada, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Understanding the patterns and processes of diversification of life in the planet is a key challenge of science. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002857:
Shaun E. Grosskurth and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of emergence of xin demarcates a key innovation in heart evolution. The catalog record names Shaun E. Grosskurth first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The mouse Xin repeat-containing proteins (mXinα and mXinβ) localize to the intercalated disc in the heart. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002957:
Cesar Bonilla, Aldo Crossa, Hector Jave and co-authors reported outcomes for extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis in Peru in 2008. XDR-TB resists most of the drugs used against tuberculosis, and many assumed cure was out of reach. Peru kept a national registry for multidrug-resistant cases over more than ten years.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team describes how often XDR-TB appeared in that registry and gives treatment outcomes for a cohort of patients. Their title states the core message: cure is possible. That evidence matters for programs deciding whether to fund full treatment for the hardest cases.
plos-pone-0003057:
R. Alexander Bentley charted academic keywords over time as an evolution problem in 2008. Keyword frequencies were recorded in the ISI Web of Science citation database. Across four case studies, change in keyword frequency through time was compared with a model of random copying.

The question contrasts random drift with selection in academic vocabulary. If copying alone explains the patterns, fashionable terms need no quality advantage to spread. Published in PLOS ONE, the analysis treats science's own language with the tools of evolution, a check on how fields convince themselves. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003157:
Nelson J. R. Fagundes, Ricardo Kanitz and Sandro L. Bonatto revisit the first peopling of the Americas in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Americas were the last continents humans settled, and many details of that process remain disputed or unknown. One hard topic is how the early settlement of Beringia, the land bridge region, actually unfolded.

The authors re-evaluate diversity in Native American mitochondrial genomes and what it implies for models of early colonization. Readers get a fresh check on a long debated history using genetic evidence. The study shows how DNA from living peoples can still test stories about ancient migration.
plos-pone-0003257:
Philippe A. Parone, Sandrine Da Cruz, Daniel Tondera and colleagues block mitochondrial division in cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria form a highly dynamic tubular network, whose morphology is regulated by frequent fission and fusion events. However, the role of mitochondrial fission in homeostasis of the organelle was still unknown. The team report the effects of preventing fission.

The title gives the outcome: preventing mitochondrial fission impairs mitochondrial function and leads to loss of mitochondrial DNA. Readers learn that constant division is not waste but upkeep. That insight bears on diseases where mitochondrial dynamics fail, from nerve to muscle disorders.
plos-pone-0003357:
Guohui Ding, Zhonghao Yu, Jing Zhao and colleagues build a tree of life from genome context in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Efforts in phylogenomics have greatly improved understanding of the backbone tree of life. However, due to systematic error in sequence data, a sequence-based phylogenomic approach leads to well-resolved but statistically significant incongruence. An independent test was therefore needed.

The authors propose a tree of life based on genome context networks. Readers get a phylogeny drawn from gene neighbourhood and context, not raw sequence alone. Agreement between two different data types would strengthen confidence in the deepest branches of life.
plos-pone-0007457:
Mariane Schleimann and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on human herpesvirus 6B, a widespread virus that infects most people in childhood. A related virus carries a gene whose protein has been linked to tumor formation in lab tests. The counterpart gene in the 6B virus, called dr6, was less understood. The team characterized the protein it encodes.

They found the DR6 protein gathers in the nucleus of infected cells. There it forms a complex with p41, the viral factor that helps copy viral DNA. That partnership ties DR6 to the virus's replication machinery. Each mapped interaction exposes a possible point of attack for antiviral drugs. The study adds one more piece to the picture of how this common virus copies itself.
plos-pone-0007557:
Pietro Mazzoni and Nancy Wexler published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how people control reaching movements. A reach can be guided attentively, with conscious correction, or automatically, without thought. Explicit control tends to engage when a movement is new. Implicit control allows several actions to run at once. The two systems are usually assessed indirectly, and this study examined them side by side.

The authors show that explicit and implicit control operate in parallel during reaching. Both steer the arm at the same time, rather than taking turns. That two-pilot picture changes how motor learning should be modeled. It matters for rehabilitation, where retraining one system may not fix the other. The study gives movement science a cleaner account of how a simple reach is governed.
plos-pone-0007657:
Xiao Li Shi and colleagues published a survey in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the smallest photosynthetic life in the southeast Pacific. Photosynthetic picoeukaryotes, cells under three micrometers wide, drive much of the ocean's primary production. Molecular methods had begun to reveal their communities. The open ocean there is oligotrophic, poor in nutrients, and vast. The team censused the tiny eukaryotes in those waters by their DNA.

Most of the community belonged to groups with no cultured representatives. The ocean's primary production in that region rests on organisms science has never grown. That fact humbles laboratory-based oceanography. DNA surveys reveal a workforce that experiments cannot yet touch. Knowing who is there is the first step toward knowing what they do. The study charts the unknown majority of a marine desert.
plos-pone-0007757:
Christopher Brower and Alexander Varshavsky published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines mice missing a protein-tagging step called arginylation. Cells mark some proteins for destruction through the N-end rule pathway. That marking needs an arginine tag, added by the enzyme Ate1.

Mice lacking this step lost fat and burned energy at a higher rate. Their sperm production was damaged. Their brains also showed disturbances. One small chemical tag thus touches body weight, fertility and brain function. The study maps how far a single protein-editing step reaches into whole-animal biology.
plos-pone-0007857:
Hiroaki Kimura and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It traces the origin of odd thyroid cells called oncocytes, or Hurthle cells. These cells appear in thyroid tumors and autoimmune disease. They look swollen, with heaps of granular cytoplasm and a dark nucleus.

Why they form had remained unknown. Using transgenic mice and human samples, the team points to overactive immunoproteasomes. These are protein-shredding machines tuned for immune defense. Their excess underlies both the oncocyte pattern and primary hypothyroidism in the study. The finding connects an immune machine to a classic thyroid puzzle.
plos-pone-0007957:
Kevin Parsons and colleagues stress-tested a common math tool for comparing species, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool, principal components analysis, shrinks many traits into a few axes for easy plotting. Biologists use it to ask whether groups evolved in like or unlike ways.

The team showed the tool has real limits when used to build a shared trait space. Plots can look neat while hiding what truly sets groups apart, which can mislead claims about chance and selection. Their warning helps researchers pick better ways to compare how lineages diverged.
plos-pone-0008057:
Matthias Dehmer and colleagues graded dozens of scores that claim to measure how complex a molecule is, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Such scores boil a chemical's tangle down to one number, which drug designers use to sort candidates. Many scores exist, but their true worth was murky.

Tested on large sets of real structures, some scores split molecules into clear, useful kinds while others mostly echoed each other or added noise. The grading lets designers drop the weak scores and keep a short, trusted set. Cleaner sorting early can save costly lab work later.
plos-pone-0008157:
Philip Leopold and colleagues measured the airway's cleaning hairs in smokers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cilia are tiny moving hairs that sweep mucus, dust, and germs out of the airways. Smokers clear that mucus poorly, and past work blamed damaged or slow-beating hairs.

Smokers' cilia proved shorter than those of non-smokers. Short hairs sweep weakly, however well they beat. Length thus joins the list of what smoking takes from the lung. Whether length returns after quitting is an open question for lung clinics. Shorter hairs also clear less of the tar and germ load each breath brings in.
plos-pone-0008257:
Helena del Corral and colleagues studied tuberculosis risk in Colombia in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. People living with a tuberculosis patient face high risk of infection. They also face risk of developing disease early. Finding who is most at risk is a goal for tuberculosis control. Blood tests based on interferon-gamma help detect infection.

The team measured interferon-gamma responses to the tuberculosis bacterium in household contacts. They related those responses to later infection and disease. A test that flags high-risk contacts could focus preventive treatment. The study supports smarter follow-up in homes of patients.
plos-pone-0008357:
Toshinori Hinoue and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a mark found in some bowel cancers. A set of bowel tumors shows a trait in which many gene sites gain a small chem tag, known as methylation. The set of sites hit is more or less the same in each such tumor. A changed gene named BRAF, in a form called V600E, shows up most times in the same tumors. The tie between the trait and that gene form called for a close look.

They mapped the tags at a large set of gene sites in the tumors. Wide maps show how firm and how tight the tie is. Tag forms may help sort bowel cancers for the right care. The work adds fine points to the chart of this cancer's types.
plos-pone-0008457:
Michael Wallner and co-authors study birch pollen allergy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Allergy to the main birch pollen protein, Bet v 1, is a top cause of spring hay fever. It affects many people in mild zones of the north. Natural Bet v 1 is a mix of many close forms. Those forms may not act the same on the immune system.

The team make forms in the lab and compare them with natural ones. They test how each form triggers immune cells and antibodies. The work shows that lab-made forms can behave unlike natural mixes. That matters for allergy tests and for shots that retrain the immune system.
plos-pone-0008557:
Anna Cogen and co-authors study a toxin from a skin germ in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Peptides that kill germs are a key part of host defense. A common skin germ, Staphylococcus epidermidis, makes such peptides. One is called delta-toxin. These peptides act on germ membranes and can kill other germs. The team test delta-toxin against Group A Streptococcus. That germ causes strep throat and more severe disease.

They find delta-toxin works with host peptides to kill the germ. The pair works better than either one alone. A friendly skin germ thus helps the host fight a harmful one. Skin germs act as active guards, not just passive guests.
plos-pone-0008657:
Peter Mumby and co-authors test marine reserves in the Caribbean in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The fisheries and biodiversity benefits of marine reserves are widely recognised. There is mounting interest in using herbivorous fishes to help ecosystems recover from climate impacts. Grazing fish keep algae from smothering corals after bleaching. Reserves that ban fishing should boost those grazers. The team compare coral recovery inside and outside Caribbean reserves.

They find marine reserves enhance the recovery of corals on those reefs. Protected reefs regain coral cover faster after disturbance. Herbivorous fish are a key link in that recovery. Reserves thus serve as a climate adaptation tool, not just a fisheries one.
plos-pone-0008757:
Rui Guo and Jun Ren examined how fast alcohol breakdown can harm the heart. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Heavy drinking weakens heart muscle in many people. A breakdown product, acetaldehyde, is a prime suspect for that damage. An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase speeds the making of that product. Mice engineered around this enzyme let the team test cause and effect.

Faster breakdown deepened heart dysfunction after alcohol exposure. Damage inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants, grew worse as well. A cell-death pathway in mitochondria carried part of the injury. Slowing that pathway might shield drinkers' hearts.
plos-pone-0008857:
Eriko Kage-Nakadai, Hiroyuki Kobuna, Masako Kimura, and colleagues guarded the worm's outer skin with two fat-handling genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Every multi-celled animal needs a surface barrier to hold its inner world together. In mammals that barrier is the outer skin layer. A protein called FATP4 is key to building it. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans uses a cuticle instead, with similar fat chemistry.

Two genes, acs-20 and acs-22, proved necessary for the cuticle barrier. Worms lacking them leaked and struggled to keep their inner balance. The worm genes mirror the mammal system closely. Barrier biology can thus be studied cheaply in worms.
plos-pone-0008957:
Olivier Roux and co-authors reported a recruiting signal that ant watchers had missed, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The African weaver ant Oecophylla longinoda rules the treetops where it lives. Workers call nestmates to food or battle with scents and body marks. Known signals included anal spots and trails laid by dragging the abdomen.

Close watching revealed workers also rub their jaws against the ground while recruiting. The jaw-rubbing deposits a signal that helps guide nestmates to the goal. It had been overlooked because the motion is small and quick. Finding it fills a gap in how this well-studied ant organises its workforce.
plos-pone-0009057:
Malgorzata Miller and co-authors introduced a staph enzyme as a first of its kind, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proline-directed kinases run many processes in human and other eukaryotic cells. MAP kinases are the best known members of that family. Such signalling enzymes were long thought to belong to eukaryotes alone.

The Staphylococcus enzyme PknB proved to be a proline-directed kinase. It is the first clear bacterial example of this class. Bacteria apparently run versions of signalling once thought uniquely complex. The find could matter medically, since staph kinases may offer drug targets.
plos-pone-0009157:
Anne-Laure Daniau and co-authors tested whether early humans burned land on purpose, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mastering fire is cast as a key innovation of early modern humans. That control may have helped them spread across the world. Some proposed our ancestors, and Neanderthals too, used fire to manage ecosystems.

The team read the charcoal record left in ancient sediments. Fire use for landscape management should leave a distinctive signal there. Comparing Neanderthal and modern human periods tested the claim. The verdict shapes how deliberate we picture Stone Age burning.
plos-pone-0009257:
Yrsa Bergmann Sverrisdóttir and co-authors published this physiology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The sympathetic nervous system, which readies the body for action, also talks to blood vessel linings. Animal work shows the two systems interact to control circulation. In humans, that interaction was largely unexplored.

The team measured muscle sympathetic nerve activity in healthy people. They compared it with a stand-in marker of endothelial function, how well vessel linings work. The two measures were related. That link in healthy volunteers sets a baseline for studying diseases where both nerves and vessels misbehave, such as hypertension.
plos-pone-0009357:
Laura Perin and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Acute tubular necrosis kills the lining cells of the kidney's tubules. The damage often leaves patients with severe kidney failure. Stem cell therapies might offer a new way to repair it.

The team tested stem cells taken from human amniotic fluid. They used mice lacking immune defenses, so the human cells could survive. The transplanted cells protected the kidneys against acute tubular necrosis. That protection in a mouse model supports the idea that these easy-to-collect cells could one day treat sudden kidney injury.
plos-pone-0011457:
Syed Meeran, Shweta Patel, and Trygve Tollefsbol reported in 2010 that a broccoli compound can silence a cancer gene without changing its code. Sulforaphane, the sharp-tasting chemical in broccoli and related vegetables, has long interested cancer researchers. The team tested its effect on hTERT, the telomerase gene that lets cancer cells divide without limit, in human breast cancer cell lines.

Sulforaphane lowered hTERT activity through epigenetic repression, chemical marks that switch a gene off while leaving its letters intact. Switching off an immortality gene with a food-derived compound is a striking lead. The authors' result comes from cells in dishes, not from diets, and that gap remains wide. Still, the work shows a concrete mechanism by which a plant chemical can reach a central cancer switch.
plos-pone-0011557:
Morio Ueyama and co-authors modeled a severe human disease in fruit flies in 2010 and found muscle precursors dying in excess. Walker-Warburg syndrome is a congenital muscular dystrophy with grave brain and eye defects, and children with it rarely survive long. A fly model lets researchers watch the disease's cell biology quickly and test its genes one by one.

In the fly model, myoblasts, the precursor cells that build muscle, died by apoptosis at increased rates. Dying precursors explain a muscle that never builds properly, linking the syndrome's genetics to a concrete cellular failure. A fast model with a clear readout, precursor death, is exactly what screening for suppressor genes and candidate drugs requires. The study gives a cruel human disease a workable laboratory handle.
plos-pone-0011657:
Cathal Seoighe and Chris Gehring asked whether people inherit differences in RNA quality control, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells destroy faulty RNA messages through a pathway called nonsense-mediated decay. Messages that keep an intron by mistake usually gain an early stop signal and are shredded by this system.

The authors measured how efficiently this decay works across individuals and tested whether the variation runs in families. They found a heritable component to decay efficiency in humans. Inherited differences in basic message clean-up could help explain why the same RNA faults affect people unevenly.
plos-pone-0011757:
Sara Branco and Richard Ree surveyed fungi living on plant roots in harsh serpentine soils, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stressful environments usually host few and highly specialised species. Serpentine soils, rich in heavy metals, impose well-known hardships on plants, but their effect on other organisms was poorly understood.

Using combined field and genetic methods, the authors measured diversity of mycorrhizal fungi, the root partners that trade nutrients with plants. Diversity was not reduced by the harsh soil. The thriving partnerships show that this underground teamwork survives even ground that is toxic to many plants.
plos-pone-0011857:
Xin-He Lai and colleagues studied in 2010 how a dangerous bacterium gets taken in by mouse immune cells. They worked with Francisella novicida, a close relative of the germ that causes tularemia, a serious fever disease. Macrophages normally swallow and kill such bacteria, yet Francisella can survive the encounter.

By testing bacterial mutants, the team found changes that alter the way macrophages carry out the swallowing process. A different route in can mean a different fate for the germ once inside. Pinpointing which bacterial genes change that route helps explain how Francisella slips past a key immune defense, and it marks steps that future treatments might try to block.
plos-pone-0011957:
Wilbert Vermeij and Claude Backendorf reported in 2010 that proteins of hardened skin do double duty during wound healing. Healing follows a set sequence from a small scratch to major injury, and reactive oxygen species, aggressive oxygen-based molecules, play roles at several stages. Too much of them damages tissue; too little stalls repair.

The team found that skin cornification proteins, the building material of the skin's tough outer layer, link oxygen detoxification with the cell migration that closes wounds. One protein system serving both cleanup and movement ties two healing steps together. That connection suggests wound treatments could target the shared machinery rather than each step separately.
plos-pone-0012057:
Yasushi Noguchi and co-workers fed mice in 2010 a diet rich in ketogenic essential amino acids and watched their livers stay lean. Fatty liver, or hepatic steatosis, builds when fat synthesis outruns fat burning. The molecular conversation between these amino acids and lipid metabolism was not fully mapped.

Their diet, with a high ratio of essential to non-essential amino acids, modulated lipid synthetic pathways and prevented fat accumulation in the liver. A dietary pattern that switches off the liver's fat-making program is a candidate strategy against a very common condition. The study also shows amino acid balance, not just calories, talking to metabolism.
plos-pone-0012157:
Ryan Edwards and Jennifer Roff re-examined claims that older fathers harm children's thinking skills, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Recent studies had linked advanced father age to weaker scores in children, a worrying pattern as parents everywhere delay having kids. But older fathers differ from younger ones in other ways too, including who they partner with and how many children they already have.

Once the mother's education and the number of siblings were taken into account, the apparent harm from father's age could be explained away. The paper is a caution against reading a simple pattern as a cause. It also steadies a debate where alarming headlines can outrun what the data really show.
plos-pone-0012257:
Hélène Foussard, Pierre Ferrer, Philippe Valenti, and co-authors introduced a new family of cell-skeleton regulators in PLOS ONE in 2010. Comparing genomes across animals reveals thousands of conserved proteins whose jobs nobody has tested. The LRCH proteins were one such blank spot: present across species, built with parts that hint at scaffolding, but functionally unknown.

The team's experiments place this family among the regulators of the cytoskeleton, the cell's inner frame of rods and ropes. Naming a family's trade is the first step toward finding which diseases involve it. Biology's catalog still holds many such untested proteins, and each characterized family shrinks that unknown map.
plos-pone-0012357:
Janine Kimpel, Stephen Braun, Gang Qiu and fellow researchers tested gene-based ways to shield T cells from HIV in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Many lab-made blockers can slow HIV in a dish, but few studies had compared them head to head. The team also asked whether protected cells gain an edge and outlive unprotected ones once HIV attacks.

They placed a membrane-bound fusion blocker into CD4 T cells, the very cells HIV targets, and infected the mix. Cells carrying the blocker survived while others died off, so the protected group took over. That survival edge is exactly what a gene therapy needs: a small dose of guarded cells could grow into lasting defense.
plos-pone-0012457:
Sarah Bush and Johannes Schul tracked mating songs in katydids, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Male songs bring the sexes together, and new song traits are usually credited to female taste. In the katydid genus Neoconocephalus, some males evolved novel call features even though females showed no preference for them.

The study argues that other forces, such as predator pressure or habitat acoustics, can drive song change without female choice. That widens the standard story of sexual selection. It reminds biologists that mating signals answer to survival needs too, not only to the preferences of the listening sex.
plos-pone-0012557:
Susanna Dunachie, Tamara Berthoud, Sheila Keating and colleagues searched for immune signs that track malaria vaccine success, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Malaria still kills huge numbers, and a vaccine is urgently needed, yet no proven correlate of protection exists — no blood sign that certifies a vaccine worked. Trial teams must wait for infections to judge success.

The chemokine MIG and the calming cytokines IL-10 and TGF beta correlated with both immunogenicity and efficacy in their vaccine trials. Candidate correlates like these, if confirmed, would let developers compare vaccine versions in weeks rather than seasons. That speed is crucial in a field with many designs and few resources.
plos-pone-0012657:
Dozmorov, Guthridge, Hurst and co-authors built a yardstick for the many ways of reading gene activity data. New lab and maths methods for expression data appear constantly, and choosing among them is hard. Their 2010 paper offers a single, broad method for scoring how well each analysis performs.

A shared yardstick lets labs compare old and new methods on equal terms. That matters because the method chosen can change which genes a study calls important. Fair scoring brings order to a crowded field and raises trust in published gene lists.
plos-pone-0012757:
Bentley, Asselbergs, Coffey and co-authors tested how gene variants from three blood systems combine to shape heart risk. The systems govern clot breakdown, blood vessel tightening and related pressure control. Earlier work had linked single genes in these systems to heart disease, with mixed results across studies.

Their 2010 study looked at the interplay among the variants rather than each one alone. Risk that only appears when several variants coincide would explain why single-gene studies disagreed. The approach reflects how the body actually works, with systems acting together rather than in isolation.
pmc-2803857:
Camacho, Coulouris, Avagyan, and co-authors introduce BLAST+, a rebuilt version of the classic sequence search tool. Searching for similar sequences is a central task in bioinformatics. BLAST uses smart shortcuts to beat exact methods, but the older software was too slow for very long queries or huge databases.

The new architecture speeds searches and splits the suite into focused programs that are easier to run at scale. Faster search matters because sequence databases grow relentlessly. BLAST+ kept a trusted method usable in the era of whole-genome queries and massive public archives.
pmc-3000457:
Gold, Ayers, Bertino, and co-authors present an aptamer-based technology for measuring many proteins at once in biomarker discovery. Studying whole sets of proteins in a multiplexed, efficient way remained a coveted but hard goal in biology and medicine. Aptamers are short molecules built to bind specific proteins.

Their technology uses such binders to measure thousands of proteins in a single sample. Wide measurement from small samples could reveal disease signatures earlier than single tests allow. The work helped open large-scale protein screening for studies of disease risk, drug response, and ageing.
pmc-3041657:
Chen and Boutros introduce VennDiagram, an R package for drawing highly customisable Venn and Euler diagrams. Biologists often need pictures of disjoint or overlapping datasets side by side. Few tools in the R environment could automate polished, high-resolution diagrams with extensive control.

Their package fills that gap, letting users tune colours, labels, and layout for publication. Overlapping sets appear in everything from gene lists to patient groups. A dependable drawing tool saves hours of manual work and reduces misleading figures in papers and presentations.  Publication-ready output removed the need to redraw diagrams in separate graphics programs.
pmc-4401657:
De Leeuw, Mooij, Heskes, and their colleagues introduced MAGMA in 2015. Gene and gene-set analysis add value to genome-wide studies by grouping marker data in a biologically sensible way. Existing methods for this task, the authors note, suffered from several issues.

MAGMA offers a generalized approach that handles genes and whole sets in one frame. It aims to be fast, flexible, and sound where older tools had gaps. Grouping signals by gene can reveal effects too weak to see marker by marker. That helps researchers connect statistical hits to real biology in traits such as brain and metabolic disorders.
pmc-5210557:
Gaulton, Hersey, Nowotka, and their team updated the ChEMBL database in 2017. ChEMBL is a large open store of bioactivity data: tests of how compounds act on living targets. First reports on it came out in 2012 and 2014, and it has grown since then.

The team kept mining the drug chemistry literature for new test results. They also added new sources of data on how compounds bind and act. A user can look up a compound or a target and see all its known test values in one place. Drug teams use that pooled data to pick leads and train models that predict new drugs.
pmc-5367557:
Griffiths, Johnson, Carducci, and their team ran a trial in 2016 of psilocybin for patients with life-threatening cancer. Such patients often face deep, lasting depression and anxiety. Early small studies had hinted that psilocybin, a psychedelic drug, might ease that distress.

The trial was randomized and double-blind, so neither patients nor staff knew who got the drug or the control at the time. The title reports large and lasting drops in depression and anxiety after the drug. Proof of this grade was rare in psychedelic research at the time. The results helped reopen medical study of psychedelics for distress at the end of life.
pmc-5472757:
Vanpouille-Box, Alard, Aryankalayil, and their colleagues reported in 2017 on radiotherapy and tumor immunity. Researchers are testing whether radiotherapy can make immunotherapy work better. The mechanisms by which radiation induces anti-tumor T cells, though, remained unclear.

The team shows that an enzyme called Trex1, a DNA exonuclease, is induced by radiation doses above a certain threshold in different cancer types. Trex1 chews up the DNA debris that would otherwise alert the immune system. That finding explains why dose per treatment matters for immune effects. It guides how radiation schedules should be designed when the goal is to partner with immunotherapy.
pmc-5891557:
Caroline Terwee and colleagues set out COSMIN methods for judging content validity in 2018. Content validity asks whether a patient questionnaire covers what matters to patients. The authors call it the most important trait of such a measure, and the hardest to judge.

Built through a Delphi process with experts, the standards rate how well a questionnaire was designed. They also rate studies that test whether items are relevant, complete, and clear. Poor content cannot be fixed by good statistics later. The guidance helps reviewers and developers build measures that patients find meaningful.
pmc-5897557:
Daniel Rosenblum, Nitin Joshi, Wei Tao, and coauthors reviewed targeted delivery of cancer drugs in 2018. Tiny carriers can ferry drugs toward tumors and spare healthy tissue. Lab studies of such carriers have multiplied over recent decades.

Yet very few carriers have reached approved clinical use, and none using active targeting had done so at the time. The authors examine why success in animals so often fails in patients. Tumor diversity and weak delivery into tumor tissue are key barriers. Their sober account helps researchers design carriers with a real chance in the clinic.
pmc-6984357:
Diego Darriba, David Posada, Alexey Kozlov, and coauthors presented ModelTest-NG in 2019. Choosing the right evolutionary model is a required step before building trees from DNA or protein data. Older tools for that choice were slow on big alignments.

ModelTest-NG rebuilds two popular predecessors from scratch. It runs one to two orders of magnitude faster while matching their accuracy. Parallel processing lets it handle genome-scale data on clusters. Phylogenetics teams folded it into standard pipelines, where model choice no longer eats the project's time budget. The tool supports both cluster machines and single workstations through the same command line.
pmc-7025157:
Marc Arbyn, Elisabet Weiderpass, Laia Bruni, and coauthors estimated cervical cancer worldwide for 2018 in this 2019 analysis. Lasting infection with human papillomavirus is the main cause of this cancer. Vaccines and virus-based screening now exist to prevent it.

The World Health Organization had just launched a global push for elimination. The authors give case and death estimates for countries around the world. Burden falls heaviest on low income countries with weak screening. Their baseline shows exactly where vaccine and screening scale-up would save the most lives. Regional tables expose deep gaps between high-burden and low-burden countries on every measure.
pmc-8265157:
Ivica Letunic and Peer Bork presented version five of the Interactive Tree Of Life in 2021, an online tool for drawing and annotating evolutionary trees. Phylogenetic trees show how species or genes are related, and researchers need to display them with layers of extra data attached. The tool is free and open to anyone through a web browser.

The new version introduces a completely rebuilt tree display engine, along with many added features for styling and annotation. The authors walk through what the engine makes possible, from huge trees to richly labeled figures for publication. Tools like this one turn the abstract output of evolutionary analysis into pictures that scientists can reason with.
plos-pone-0360057:
Qian Zhu and co-authors applied and evaluated in 2026 a system of quality indicators for pharmaceutical care in pain management around orthopedic surgery. Patients recovering from bone and joint operations need pain relief that is effective yet safe, and pharmacists play a central part in getting doses and drug choices right. A quality indicator system sets measurable standards for that care, so hospitals can see where practice falls short.

The authors describe building the indicator set for the perioperative period, the span before, during, and after surgery, and testing how it performs in use. Systems like this turn good intentions into checkable routines. They also give hospitals a fair way to compare units and track improvement over time.
plos-pone-0343857:
Sarah Alkhatib and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about research funding. Grant abstracts submitted to the NIH, the United States National Institutes of Health, are often coded by hand, meaning readers sort them into categories. The authors compare that human coding with coding done by artificial intelligence.

A head-to-head comparison shows where machine coding matches trained readers and where it drifts. Coding thousands of abstracts is slow, costly work, so a reliable automated option would change how agencies track their research portfolios. Science administrators and research evaluators are the natural audience for this test of AI against human judgment.
plos-pone-0358257:
Eirette Santiago and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plant defense. Plants can react to a warning cue that an attack is coming, before any insect actually feeds. The authors study responses that are specific to the herbivore involved, rather than one general alarm.

A pre-attack risk cue lets a plant prepare defenses early, but preparing the wrong defense wastes resources. Testing whether responses match the coming herbivore shows how finely plants can read these signals. Ecologists and crop scientists share an interest here, since pest warning systems in farming rest on the same idea of early, targeted defense.
plos-pone-0359657:
Alison McAfee and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It examines honey bee queens imported into Canada from around the globe. The authors record pheromone features, the chemical signals a queen produces, alongside morphometric features, precise measurements of her body.

Queen quality decides how well a colony thrives, and Canadian beekeepers import many queens each year. Comparing chemical and physical traits across source countries tells buyers and regulators what differs between suppliers. Beekeepers choosing stock, and scientists studying queen health, both gain from a profile of what imported queens actually look like.
plos-pone-0359957:
Sudarshawn Damodharan and James Tonsgard wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review, combined with a meta-analysis, of MEK inhibitors, a class of targeted drugs. The patients are people with NF1, a genetic condition, who have symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas, tumors growing along nerves that surgery cannot safely remove.

The review weighs efficacy and safety together across the available studies. Families facing these disfiguring and painful tumors have few options, so a careful pooling of drug evidence guides real treatment choices. Neurologists and oncologists who manage NF1 are the readers who need this balanced summary.
plos-pone-0337157: Lashley and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study testing whether rats can model Gulf War illness. Male Sprague-Dawley rats from Charles River faced several chemical and stress setups drawn from war exposures. The title reports the result with care: signs like those of the illness showed up only in limited ways. A weak animal model warns researchers to rethink how they test causes and cures.
plos-pone-0343457: Zhang and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that sorts brain tumor scans. Their system aims to name tumor types with high accuracy. A design feature called complementary downsampling blocks helps the system keep fine detail while shrinking images for speed. Fast, accurate scan sorting could help doctors in busy hospitals decide sooner which patients need urgent care.
plos-pone-0358557: Munna and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on artificial intelligence in women's reproductive health. As a scoping review, it maps global trends in diagnosis tools. It also names gaps in methods and sets an agenda for putting tools to work where resources are scarce. AI tests that only work in rich hospitals leave most of the world out.
plos-pone-0356757:
Thomas U Grund, writing in PLOS ONE in 2026, asks whether a well known quirk of the mind also shapes whole crowds. People tend to dwell on bad news more than good news, a pattern called negativity bias. Grund tests whether fan communities focus their dislike on a few targets while spreading their affection much more widely.

He studies reports from more than thirty-six thousand German football fans about the clubs they love and hate. Dislike turned out to be far more tightly focused than affection, both in what fans sent out and in what clubs received. Love and hate also moved mostly independently of each other. The result suggests that the structure of rivalry, and of conflict more broadly, is built into how groups divide their attention.

europmc-pmc7378357: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on crosstalk between astrocytes and microglia (the brain's immune cells): an survey. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8234057: Chen and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on control of neurotransmitters by the gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) and effects on cognition in neurological illnesses. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8329257: A fresh look at tumor microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor) and immune evasion in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (a common type of cancer) arrived with this 2021 research paper. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (a common type of cancer), an aggressive malignancy, is characterized by high sickness. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8593957: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on moms are not OK: COVID-19 and maternal mental health. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
the-last-of-the-mohicans-a-narrative-of-: James Fenimore Cooper's 1826 frontier classic: during the French and Indian War, Hawkeye the scout guides two sisters through ambushes and sieges, while Uncas, the last of the Mohicans, fights beside him. Stirring, romantic, and deeply American, it created the Western hero and has never left the public imagination.
mistress-wilding-pg1457: Rafael Sabatini's 1924 tale of Monmouth's doomed rising in 1685: a young English gentleman is torn between loyalty to his love and duty to his cause. Dashing swordplay, court intrigue, and narrow escapes move at Sabatini's irresistible clip. Historical romance from the master of the swashbuckler.
king-richard-iii-pg2257: The ghosts gather in this edition: on Bosworth's eve the murdered visit Richard's tent, each crying "Despair and die." He wakes to battle and his famous cry for a horse. The villain-hero's last night, terrifying and magnificent.
pages-from-an-old-volume-of-life-a-colle: Oliver Wendell Holmes's pages from an old volume of life: essays from 1857 to 1881. The Autocrat's wisdom gathered, mellow and bright. A lifetime's table talk. Holmes's old volume is wisdom mellowed with age, a lifetime's bright talk.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume seven of Casanova's memoirs: adventures continue apace. The Venetian's luck holds. The story's early prime. Seventh volume: luck holds, the story's early prime, the story's bright early prime, adventures crowd his days, the young rover's luck holds.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of: This Saint-Simon volume chronicles the pride of the great nobles. The passionate duke defends his order's ancient privileges fiercely. Quarrels over precedence become epic battles. Aristocratic pride displayed in its fullest and finest flower.
plos-pone-0358357:
Koray Samet Altınçekiç leads a team of eight testing whether a minute of foam rolling sharpens young basketball players' reactions, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One hundred two male players aged sixteen to eighteen were assigned to roll for thirty seconds per body region, sixty seconds, or simply rest. Hand reaction time to a visual signal was measured before and after, with the best single trial as the headline score.

The shorter rolling dose beat the longer one clearly across best, average, and median scoring. Against rest, the advantage reached significance only on the best trial analysis, not on average or median performance, and one standard statistical model broke its own assumptions, forcing a bootstrap recheck. The authors' honest summary is mixed: brief foam rolling may sharpen a player's single fastest response, but claims of a broad reaction boost outrun this evidence.
plos-pone-0357457:
Guillaume P Fernandez, Eric D Widmer, and Robin Dodsworth ask whether the company around a conversation changes how speakers talk, in PLOS ONE in 2026. People unconsciously match a partner's way of speaking to signal closeness, a habit called linguistic accommodation. Most research treats that matching as a private affair between two people. This team suspected the speaker's wider personal network shapes it too.

Twenty-one young adults recorded themselves across seventy-one conversations and mapped their personal networks. The researchers measured matching through the use of intensifier words, those small boosters like really and so. Speakers matched more when their partner sat at the center of a dense, uniform cluster inside the speaker's network, a tight subgroup drawn from one social world. Accommodation, it turns out, answers not just to the person in front of you, but to the audience standing behind them.
plos-pone-0358457:
Juliana Ofosua Addo leads a team of eight measuring fear of childbirth among pregnant women in Kumasi, Ghana, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred eighty-two women attending antenatal care at a primary facility completed a standard fear questionnaire. The authors deliberately split their analysis by parity, whether a woman had given birth before, arguing that first time mothers and experienced mothers fear different things and need different support.

About twenty-two percent of the women scored in the high to severe fear range. First time mothers reported clearly higher fear than those who had delivered before. When the team modeled what drives fear inside each group separately, the determinants differed by parity, matching their opening argument. A first time mother's fear grows from the unknown; a returning mother's often grows from memory. Antenatal programs that treat the two as one audience, the authors imply, will comfort neither well.
plos-pone-0358657:
Fukai Zhao leads a team of seven refining how scans predict who will benefit from bypass surgery, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In ischemic cardiomyopathy, parts of the heart muscle are starved but still alive, hibernating rather than dead. Surgery helps those patients most, and PET scans can map living tissue. The standard mismatch reading is contested, so the team compared it with a simpler ratio drawn from the same scans in fifty-three patients who went on to bypass operations.

About sixty percent of patients regained meaningful pumping strength after surgery. The uptake ratio between damaged and healthy zones predicted that recovery well, clearly beating the conventional mismatch index for the more common recovery threshold. It did not predict later major cardiac events. The authors call the ratio a useful quantitative companion to the standard reading, while asking for larger multi center validation before it guides who gets an operation.
plos-pone-0357057:
Donghuan Bai, Xiaodong Cao, and Shuolei Feng studied a common running injury in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Marathon runners often develop pain around the kneecap, called patellofemoral pain syndrome. Weak hips are one suspect, since hip control affects how the knee tracks during each stride.

Bai and his colleagues compared records of runners given hip stability training with runners given standard care. They tracked pain and the Q-angle, a measure of knee alignment. The comparison tests whether stronger hips truly ease this pain. For coaches and physios, evidence of that kind guides whether hip work should be a routine part of treating runner's knee.
plos-pone-0344957:
Yekai Feng led a team of eight authors building a prognostic tool for head and neck cancer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These cancers need better ways to predict outcomes and choose treatment. The team built an index based on PANoptosis, a combined form of cell death, and applied it to squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck.

Feng's index sorts patients by risk, and the work also revealed a gene, DSCAM, as a possible treatment target. A tool that both predicts and points to a target is doubly useful. Clinicians gain a risk score for planning, and drug researchers gain a named lead. Head and neck cancers often return after treatment, so sharper prognosis can guide how closely each patient is watched.
plos-pone-0357957:
Kuan-Ting Chen and colleagues published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE from a humanitarian medical mission that a Taiwanese hospital ran at three sites in Ukraine in April 2026. War disrupts the steady care high blood pressure needs, yet screening data from active conflict zones are rare. The team measured blood pressure in adults attending the mission and traced the care cascade: who knew their condition, who was treated, who had it controlled.

About two-thirds of adults screened had raised blood pressure on the raw count, and even after age adjustment more than half did. Rates climbed with age and were higher in men and in people with obesity. About three-quarters of those affected knew it, but fewer than six in ten were treated and only about one in six had pressure controlled. The mission model, they say, can find and reconnect patients whose care the war has broken.
plos-pone-0355557:
Camilla Mapstone, Julia Handl, and David Talavera stress-test the hope that machine learning on whole genomes can find disease-causing gene combinations. Dosage effects across many genes are thought to drive disease, but the search space is enormous. The team built benchmarks two ways. Real data came with known answers. Synthetic data came with dials for size and noise. Standard models were then trained to classify patients and to name the guilty genes.

A plain regression model proved most reliable at fingering the true genes across synthetic worlds, even when its raw classification score lagged flashier rivals. Attempts on a major biobank dataset failed outright, and digging in showed why: models stumbled unless the activity of working genes was taken into account. Mapstone and colleagues say genome-wide learners must respect which genes are actually switched on.
plos-pone-0356257:
Olivia Smith and seven colleagues check whether a lab test for filoviruses, the family that includes Ebola, gives the same answers in very different laboratories, reporting in 2026. Their bead-based test can detect antibodies against several filoviruses at once, which is valuable for tracking past infections and vaccine responses. Samples were tested both at a university lab in Hawaii and at the national research institute in Kinshasa, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Results from the two sites matched closely, with variation staying below preset limits for every target. Samples from Ebola survivors and close contacts, plus hundreds taken before and after vaccination in Congo, showed the expected patterns. Vaccine-related antibody signals rose after vaccination, while signals for other filoviruses stayed flat. The authors say the test is reproducible enough for surveillance and vaccine studies across settings.
plos-pone-0349357:
Karin van der Burg and six colleagues compare two laboratory strains of the eastern spruce budworm, a major forest pest, in this 2026 genomics study. Most budworm caterpillars pause development as tiny larvae to survive winter, a state called diapause, but a selectable minority skip it and keep growing. The team assembled a chromosome-level genome for the non-diapausing strain and compared it with the published genome and gene activity of the diapausing one.

Despite the dramatic life-history difference, the genomes showed no major rearrangements, suggesting the trait rests on small genetic differences. Gene activity, by contrast, diverged sharply: the diapausing strain ramped up genes for sugar burning and for processing environmental signals. The split in expression appeared midway through the first larval stage, before the paths visibly separate. The work narrows where researchers should hunt for diapause's genetic switches.
plos-pone-0355057:
Martin Aman and seven colleagues compare surgical strategies for preventing painful neuromas after nerve cuts, in this 2026 rat study. When a nerve is severed, its stump can sprout a disorganized, tender ball of fibers. Forty rats received either a sham operation, heat coagulation of the stump, or one of two commercial nerve caps, made of chitosan or a biodegradable plastic, over the cut sciatic nerve. Twelve weeks later the team examined the tissue directly, by MRI, and through blinded surgeon ratings.

Capped stumps formed denser, more contained neuromas with far more nerve fibers and thicker insulation than untreated stumps. Coagulation, however, matched the caps on those microscopic measures despite lumpier outward shapes, and surgeons' ratings echoed the macroscopic pattern. The authors conclude caps genuinely organize regeneration, while the simpler coagulation remains a credible option, supporting more personalized surgical choices.
plos-pone-0355957:
Khai Truong and co-authors re-tuned a DNA test for a gut parasite increasingly found on American-grown produce. Cyclospora spreads through contaminated food and water, and tracing outbreaks needs reliable environmental testing. The original assay was validated on a discontinued machine. Their 2026 study optimised it for a current laboratory platform.

Only three settings needed change: a slightly lower binding temperature, more cycles, and a later cutoff for calling a result positive. With those tweaks, the test matched the original platform's performance on spiked farm water. Checks against near-neighbour organisms guarded against false alarms. Truong and colleagues deliver a ready protocol for labs that must run the official method on modern equipment.
plos-pone-0355457:
Olusiji Adebola Lasekan and co-authors dissected how African leaders built sustainability arguments in their 2025 United Nations speeches, then turned the patterns into a teaching model. The corpus held twenty-one English speeches totalling about fifty thousand words. Their 2026 analysis worked across word choice, grammar, sentence shape, persuasive strategy, and whole-speech structure.

Meaning rode mainly on vocabulary and on how speeches were organised. Urgency and collective agency dominated the persuasive moves. Tools like obligation verbs, conditionals, and problem-then-solution sequencing mapped onto named sustainability skills. Strategic and people skills dominated the speeches. Lasekan and colleagues package the mapping as a grammar-to-sustainability classroom model for education programmes.
plos-pone-0354957:
Haoran Wang and colleagues study in 2026 what helps visitors feel restored at Mount Emei, a sacred heritage site in China. Hundreds of visitors at ten spots answered surveys, and crews also measured real sound levels on site. The team tested whether liking the site's sounds worked in part by making the place feel culturally true.

Liking the sounds linked both directly to feeling restored and to a stronger sense of cultural truth, which itself linked to restoration. Sound thus helped in two ways, through the senses and through meaning. Site managers may treat bells, chants, and natural sounds as part of care for visitors, not mere background.
plos-pone-0354857:
Lijing Yang, Wanju Wang, and Yajuan Chen apply in 2026 an explainable learning method to find what shapes how long mothers breastfeed. Records followed a modest group of mothers after birth, covering birth details, body factors, and social background. The model was built to handle tangled, non straight line links and to show which factor mixes mattered most.

The model sorted long and short feeding well, above all catching most long term cases. Risk rose when a surgical birth combined with long milk blockage, and when highly educated mothers moved to mixed feeding. The authors argue for support aimed at such specific profiles rather than general lessons for everyone.
plos-pone-0354157:
Suxiang Qin and Songwen Wei build in 2026 a combined vision and language system for studying marketing images. Their system must find brand logos in busy scenes, link pictures with their text, and judge how much viewers will like the look of an advert. Three linked parts handle detection, alignment, and a tuning method that keeps training costs low.

On public logo and beauty rating sets, their system beat well known earlier methods on detection and on predicting taste scores. It also sorted marketing success well in their tests. Brands could use such tools to check creative work before spending on a full campaign.
plos-pone-0349257:
Fábia Fernandes, Ricardo Bezerra, and Isabelle Barbosa assess in 2026 how well people with diabetes in Brazil receive proper care, and how gender, race, and income combine to shape that care. They used a national health survey covering several thousand adults who reported a diabetes diagnosis. Adequate care was judged against expected checks and referrals.

Gaps centred on foot checks and referral to specialists. Low income Black men and women had the highest rates of poor care. Oddly, people without complications or hospital stays also got less complete care. The authors name poverty and structural racism as core drivers needing policy action.
plos-pone-0354757:
Can Çelebi and Stefan Penczynski test in 2026 how well human codebooks work as prompts when large language models classify text from experiments. Three codebooks from experimental economics were used, covering promise keeping and strategic thinking. Prompt detail, format, framing, and wording were varied across two commercial and two open models, and results were compared with human annotators.

Codebooks as prompts agreed with humans at a high rate across tasks. On a recognition heavy task, model choice drove accuracy most, while on learning heavy tasks, instruction detail mattered as much. Extra content helped larger models but could hurt smaller ones. Write prompts like good human instructions, the authors urge.
plos-pone-0353357:
Ryan A Denu led a team of eight authors on this 2026 claims study of a cancer drug used in the United States. Regorafenib is approved as a later option for advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors, a rare gut cancer, after earlier targeted drugs fail. The team mined insurance records spanning 2015 to 2023 for patients who filled the drug.

Patients starting on a lower dose stayed on treatment about as long as those on the standard dose, and waited similar times before switching therapy. People who had taken only one earlier drug fared longer than those who had taken two. Denu calls for outcome studies next.
plos-pone-0344857:
Jing Wu and four colleagues published this 2026 algorithms paper on nonnegative matrix factorization, a workhorse method that breaks big data tables into simpler parts for tasks like image and text analysis. Their hybrid method alternates between two solvers, guided by a relaxed line search with a tunable looseness setting and room for larger steps.

Under mild assumptions the authors prove the method settles at a solution. On artificial and real data sets it ran more efficiently than leading rivals. Wu aims the improvement at anyone factoring large data on a deadline.
plos-pone-0327957: Black garden ants — their foraging trajectories hide search strategies. This paper discovered those behaviors in ant movement data. The findings reveal the algorithms of tiny brains — with lessons for robotics and optimization.
plos-pone-0354357:
Pons-Gomila and colleagues, in 2026, measured how hard different training tasks are for women who play basketball. Fourteen players wore tracking and heart rate gear across twenty-two weeks of practice. The team sorted drills into three kinds: drills with no opponent, small-sided games, and full competitive formats.

Small-sided games produced higher values than competitive play on almost every measure, from distance run to jumps and hard changes of speed. Drills with no opponent also beat full games on distance, bursts of speed, and jumps, though full games kept heart rates high for longer. Bigger court space raised the load for most measures as well. For coaches, the message is practical: the shape of a drill and the size of the space can tune how much strain a session puts on players.
plos-pone-0354257:
Siam and colleagues, in a 2026 study, trace the family tree of the small white butterfly, a cabbage pest found on nearly every continent. The butterfly spread worldwide through both natural flight and human trade. The team read one gene from more than a thousand samples across five continents to see how populations connect.

They found well over a hundred distinct versions of the gene. Europe held the richest mix, which fits an old home range. North America held few versions but with deep differences between them, a sign the continent was colonized more than once from different sources. Most variation sat within populations rather than between them, and distance alone did not explain the pattern. A web-like family tree, with a few very common versions at its center, points to recent rapid spread. The authors say trade routes, not just wind, wrote this pest's travel history.
plos-pone-0354457:
Majima and colleagues, in a 2026 field study, measure radiation in parts of Okuma Town, Fukushima, where residents are being allowed to return. The town sat next to the damaged nuclear plant, and some zones are set aside for returnees before homes are cleaned up or torn down. Knowing actual dose levels is basic to honest return policy.

Surveys drove radiation meters along roads across the return zones, and teams also measured at house entrances before cleanup. Road readings fell clearly between late 2024 and late 2025. At homes, yearly dose estimates for most areas sat under the government's reference level for lifting evacuation orders. They did not, however, reach the long-term target set after the accident, which is far lower. The authors offer the gap between those two benchmarks as the real policy question: safe enough to return by rule, yet above the level promised for the long run.
plos-pone-0332357:
McCurtin and colleagues, in a 2026 study, count how often doctors in England dispense thickeners for people who swallow unsafely. Thickened drinks flow more slowly, which can stop liquid entering the airway. The products are widely used, especially for older people, yet basic facts about their dispensing were missing. The team mined a national prescribing database for 2019 to 2024.

Nearly three million thickener items were dispensed in primary care over the five years, costing the health service nearly ninety million pounds. Use fell steadily among adults, who are the main users, while dispensing to babies under one rose. Costs still climbed in the last year, despite falling use in most age groups. Gum-based products made up the vast majority of items. The authors say this first map of practice raises sharp questions about when thickeners help, what they cost, and why use is shifting by age.
plos-pone-0351657:
Borianne and colleagues, in a 2026 study, race six artificial intelligence models at spotting cocoa pods in photos of farms in Côte d'Ivoire. Counting pods early helps farmers forecast harvests and bargain with buyers. Photos were low-resolution, as farm pictures often are. Models ranged from tiny versions to ones with many times more internal parts, all trained on thousands of hand-labeled pods.

The small, fast models won. Tiny versions of two YOLO designs beat the bigger transformer and classic models, scoring especially well on trees in the foreground. That upset the usual expectation that bigger is better. Reviewing why, the authors found fault in the training data itself: labels were inconsistent, and there were too few images to feed the giant models properly. The honest conclusion is two-sided: small models already work well for pod counting, and cleaner, larger teaching sets are needed before crowning any champion.
plos-pone-0352857:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, sort younger Chinese patients with high blood pressure by how well they understand their medicines. Taking daily pills for decades only works if patients grasp doses, timing, and risks. More than five hundred patients at two large hospitals answered scales on medication knowledge, social support, confidence, and how they view their illness.

A profiling method found three groups: about a third with low medication literacy, half in the middle, and a small top group. Education and household income sorted people strongly: less of each meant the low group. Rich social support, confidence in managing health, and a more hopeful view of the illness marked the top group. The authors propose tiered help: plain teaching for the lowest group, habit-building support for the middle, and lighter touch for the strongest.
plos-pone-0352457:
