Aaron Kolb and six colleagues infect mice with herpes simplex virus to test whether a protein called thrombospondin-1 shapes eye disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The protein normally helps control inflammation and blood-vessel growth in the cornea, and herpes infection there can cloud vision. Mice bred to lack the protein were compared with normal mice after their corneas were infected with two virus strains.

Disease severity, corneal clouding, vessel growth, and nerve loss were the same in both groups. Antibody and T-cell responses also matched. A severe whole-eye inflammation appeared with one strain in both kinds of mice. The negative result suggests other family proteins cover for the missing one.
plos-pone-0353757:
Michihiro Tateyama and Yoshihiro Kubo examine how the female hormone estradiol interacts with an ion channel found in immune cells of the brain, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The channel, THIK-1, lets potassium ions flow and helps control inflammation in microglia. The team applied steroids to the mouse channel in the laboratory and measured the currents that passed.

Estradiol turned the channel down by roughly forty percent. Computer docking and targeted mutations pinpointed where the hormone likely sits: a cavity above the channel's gate. Some mutations made the channel exquisitely sensitive instead, responding to far weaker hormone levels. The work hints that hormone differences could tune brain inflammation between people.
plos-pone-0349857:
John Hart and seven colleagues formally describe a new species of monkey from the forests of the Democratic Republic of Congo, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The animal, known locally as Likweli, lives between the Lomami and Congo rivers in high, closed-canopy forest. Over four years the team logged more than a hundred observations across its small estimated range, where it travels in groups of about six, often alongside other monkey species.

Genetic and anatomical evidence places it in the black colobus group, as the closest relative of a species found over a thousand kilometres away, and its calls match that kinship too. Rare, shy, and barely known even locally, the new species begins its scientific life already in need of protection.
plos-pone-0353157:
Mols and colleagues ran a one-day check of emergency care across hospitals in the Netherlands in a 2026 study. For twenty-four hours, twenty-eight hospitals recorded adults who came to emergency rooms for internal medicine care. The aim was to see how many visits grew out of long-term illness and how many could be handled elsewhere.

Nearly half of the visits involved a sudden flare of a long-term condition. About a quarter of all visits were judged avoidable, and about two in five patients could have used a clinic or direct admission unit instead. Most hospitals had such options, but poor organization blocked their use, which points to fixes in planning rather than new buildings.
plos-pone-0353457:
Murungweni and colleagues interviewed fishing stakeholders about plastic pollution at a South African reservoir in a 2026 study. Thirty people took part: commercial fishers, recreational fishers, and fish sellers around Nandoni Dam. Nearly all knew plastic pollution was a problem, yet most had only a thin grasp of microplastics.

Groups differed in who they blamed, most often pointing to visitors, with some naming local residents. Willingness to join cleanup action was also explored. Managers who understand how each group sees the problem can design campaigns that fishers support rather than ignore, since daily users witness the waste first.
plos-pone-0353257:
Hongyang Chen and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of radiomics, a technique that mines medical images for patterns predicting whether lung cancer carries a particular resistance mutation. The mutation, called T790M, blunts the effect of a major class of targeted drugs, so knowing its status guides treatment. The reviewers pooled thirteen studies covering more than twenty-six hundred patients.

Models tested on their own data performed strongly, but accuracy dropped when applied to outside patients, a common warning sign in this field. Performance also shifted with imaging type, the body site imaged, and study quality. The authors conclude that image-based prediction is promising for avoiding repeat biopsies, though better-standardized studies are needed before clinical use.
plos-pone-0352757:
Sama Koliaei and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One chemistry study of four hawthorn species. Hawthorn is valued for medicine and food. The team tested leaves and fruits of each species. They measured phenolic compounds, the plant chemicals behind hawthorn's antioxidant fame. They also measured total antioxidant strength. The question was how much species and growing site shape that chemistry.

Phenolic levels varied hugely between species. Some compounds differed several-fold. Fruit phenols and flavonoids rose together closely. Grouping placed two species near each other. A third stood clearly apart, with the richest store of key compounds. Tests linked antioxidant strength to certain phenolic families. The authors say these profiles can guide which species to develop for health products. Local growing conditions should be factored in too.
plos-pone-0352257:
Jaime Barranco and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One imaging paper on the eye. It teaches a computer to outline the eye and its socket in MRI scans. Drawing these parts by hand is slow. That has kept eye-imaging studies small. The team used scans from more than twelve hundred adults. They trained a leading deep learning system to trace five parts: the lens, the eyeball, the optic nerve, the eye muscles, and the orbital fat.

The system traced all five parts well. It could also estimate eye length and tissue volumes on its own. That let the team check how eye parts relate to body mass at scale. As a headline product, they release the first large eye atlases made without bias. There are atlases for women, for men, and for both combined. They are meant to standardize future eye MRI research.
plos-pone-0347757:
Steffen Herbold and three colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether large language models can convincingly imitate real people in political debate. They drew on Question Time, a BBC television programme where panellists answer audience questions. Then they asked language models to write replies in the panellists' place.

A cross-section of the British public then judged both versions without knowing which was which. The machine-written answers were rated more authentic, more relevant, and more coherent than the originals, and writing style did not explain the gap. The authors warn that such convincing fakes could mislead voters, so the public urgently needs warning about the risk.
plos-pone-0351757:
Juan Du and seven colleagues teach a neural network to read brain tumour scans in this 2026 study. Two traits guide glioma treatment: whether the tumour carries an IDH mutation, and how fast its cells divide, marked by Ki-67. Both normally need tissue from surgery. The team built one model that predicts both at once. It feeds on four kinds of MRI, taken within a month before surgery at two hospitals. One hospital trained the model, the other tested it independently.

Hand-crafted image measurements and clinical details were fused with the network's features. Rival models served as comparisons. Accuracy was judged with standard curves, calibration checks, and decision analysis. Explanation tools highlighted which image regions drove each prediction. Non-invasive prediction matters because some patients cannot be biopsied. A validated scan-based estimate could shape treatment planning days earlier, while sparing patients an operation whose only purpose is information.
plos-pone-0352357:
Shumani Makhadi and three colleagues pool the evidence on emergency trauma surgery in poorer countries. Their 2026 systematic review covers damage control laparotomy. The technique opens the abdomen, stops the bleeding fast, and postpones full repair. It serves patients caught in the lethal triad of cold, acidity, and failed clotting. Ten retrospective studies, covering nine hundred fourteen patients in five countries, met the criteria. South African hospitals supplied over three-quarters of the cases.

The pooled death rate landed near thirty-eight percent. Study results varied widely, with substantial statistical heterogeneity. Fragmented evidence is itself the finding. Wealthy countries document this operation thoroughly; the places carrying the heaviest trauma loads report it patchily. A pooled mortality figure gives surgeons and ministries a first benchmark for their own units. It also argues for trauma registries in low-income settings, so the next review can compare like with like.
plos-pone-0348957:
Anina van Leeuwen and colleagues lay out the plan for StepuP, a trial testing treadmill training for people with Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's stiffens walking and raises fall risk, and walking on a treadmill at varied speeds already helps in clinics. What remains unclear is how the training changes the body and brain, which this trial is built to measure.

About a hundred twenty-six patients at four sites will be assigned by chance to standard speed-based treadmill training or to an enriched version with virtual reality or sudden nudges. Brain waves, muscle signals, and three-dimensional movement will be recorded before training, after it, and three months later. Healthy older adults serve as a comparison group. No results are reported here.
plos-pone-0352157:
Jaehoon Yeom, Minji Kim, and Sang Don Kim tackled a missing number in river science. Nobody knows what most freshwater invertebrates weigh when dried. Yet weight feeds food-web models and pollution risk work. The team mined field guides and papers for length and weight records. The records covered invertebrates from Korean rivers. From them they built formulas that predict weight from length alone.

Formulas tuned at the genus level matched real weighed specimens best. Broader family and order formulas did worse. More source studies also made the formulas sharper. The team then produced reference dry weights for over five hundred kinds of invertebrates. A quick length measure can now give the living mass of a whole river sample.
plos-pone-0350657:
Root canal treatment sometimes fails because a hardy bacterium, Enterococcus faecalis, survives deep in the tooth. Daniel K Arens and co-authors collected viruses that infect this bacterium, called phages, from wastewater, and tested them as a possible treatment aid in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Fourteen phages were isolated and checked against many strains of the bacterium, including two taken from mouths. Several attacked a wide range of strains, slowed growth even at low doses, and stripped away up to ninety-seven percent of tough bacterial films. The team offers the set as fresh candidates for fighting stubborn dental infections.
plos-pone-0351557:
Baduanjin, a gentle traditional Chinese exercise of eight movements, draws loyal older practitioners. Haixu Ji and colleagues interviewed twenty-five community-dwelling older adults living with chronic diseases to learn why they keep practicing, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Five reasons held people to the routine. The movements felt safe and easy to learn. Bodies felt better with practice. Mood and mental calm improved. Group sessions widened social life. And many valued the exercise as a piece of their own traditional culture. The authors suggest community programs lean on all five draws, not health claims alone, to keep attendance high.
plos-pone-0351157:
Xin Fang and Xingyue Peng asked how United States tightening of money policy since 2022 spilled onto share prices in China. Higher United States rates and a shrinking central bank balance sheet can shake foreign markets. The pair tracked short term price moves for listed Chinese firms around tightening news, sorting each firms overseas links into trade, investment, and finance.

Trade links helped, with exposed firms gaining stronger extra returns after shocks. Investment and finance links hurt, dragging returns down. Firms with heavy foreign ownership or overseas deals fared worst. Manager skill and venture backing softened or sharpened effects in distinct ways, and tech level mattered too. Where a firm reaches abroad, not just how much, shapes its risk.
plos-pone-0345157:
Mahdieh Maazalahi and Soodeh Hosseini model how botnets, networks of hijacked computers, spread through complex computer networks. Spread is treated like a disease, with machines moving from open to exposed to infected to recovered states. Alongside the spread model, the pair built a detection system that blends learning methods with search tricks to pick telling features.

Simulations showed their spread model lowered the share of infected machines and halted spread sooner than rival models. The detector, tried on three public attack data sets, spotted attacks with accuracy in the low ninety percent range and fewer missed or false alarms. Early maths on spread helps defenders judge whether an outbreak will grow or die out.
plos-pone-0340557:
Poramad Trivalairat and colleagues assessed drinking water risks in six mountain villages above Bhumibol Dam in Thailand. Indigenous families there rely on natural sources whose dangers they may not know. Water from thirty eight sources, plus soil and edible crop parts, were tested for acidity, nitrate, and pesticide traces over six months, alongside a village filter trial.

Sources villagers liked best for drinking proved riskiest, with high nitrate, strong alkalinity, and pesticide traces likely washed from farms. Every soil sample and the underground parts of food crops carried residues, so diet adds exposure. The village filter did not improve water quality across the trial. Still puddle water, prized for taste, needs urgent safer handling.
plos-pone-0351057:
Wenze Yu and colleagues used single cell gene reading to study cells other than heart muscle in diabetic heart disease, where the heart stiffens and weakens without blocked arteries. Public cell data from diabetes and heart muscle disease were sorted into cell types, with metabolism scores, life path tracking, and cell to cell signal maps. One marker gene was then tested in vessel cells in dishes.

Eight cell types appeared, with natural killer and smooth muscle cells shared across both diseases. Immune, vessel lining, and nerve cells ranked most metabolically active. Dish tests probed how one immune marker gene affects vessel cell growth and movement. Non muscle cells, long treated as background, may drive much of diabetic heart damage.
plos-pone-0350857:
Sidartawan Soegondo and colleagues reported the Indonesian part of a large Asia Pacific survey on obesity care in 2026. A thousand adults living with obesity and two hundred health workers answered questions online about beliefs, talks, and barriers.

Views clashed. Most health workers called obesity a chronic disease, but only about half of patients did, and most patients blamed themselves while few workers did. Two thirds of patients saw themselves as merely overweight, and few had discussed weight with a clinician in five years. Money worries also blocked care. The gaps point to kinder, clearer first conversations as the place to start.
plos-pone-0350457:
Beyhan Başkan, Hatice Kübra Başkan, and Nevzat Koç tested eight leading language models on past exam questions for dentistry specialisation in Turkey in 2026. The questions covered endodontics, the root canal specialty, across a decade of national exams.

One hundred twenty-seven questions, split between knowledge and clinical cases, were put to each model and scored against official keys. Scores differed widely. The top model cleared ninety percent and beat rivals clearly on clinical cases, while the weakest sat near sixty percent. Such spread warns students and teachers that model choice, not just model use, decides study value.
plos-pone-0331157:
Maxwell Ateni Assibi and co-authors reviewed studies in 2026 on how medical students experience learning alongside other health professions. Working across professions is now a stated goal of training, yet student experience of it is patchy.

Eight studies from a decade of literature met the criteria. Students generally welcomed collaborative learning and valued contact with other professions, but grasp of each other's roles stayed shaky. Role confusion, professional hierarchy, and timetabling blocked progress, while real practice placements, curriculum integration, and staff support helped. The review gives course designers a short, evidence based list of what to fix first.
plos-pone-0347657:
Hasti Garjani, Joel S Brown, and co-authors asked which math model best matches how lung cancer cells grow and resist drugs in the lab. They used published data on non-small cell lung cancer, tracking drug-sensitive and drug-resistant cells grown alone and together, with and without the drug alectinib and helper cells called fibroblasts. Their 2026 study compared several growth curves and drug-effect formulas against the data.

A classic logistic growth model with a ratio-based drug effect fit the single-type cultures best. Carrying those settings into mixed cultures showed that fibroblasts helped both cell types live together, while the drug pushed one type out. The authors stress that a model must fit the data and also make biological sense before doctors lean on it for treatment planning.
plos-pone-0350557:
Ya-Qin You, Han-Han Song, and Yu-Liang Feng surveyed streaming video users to learn which parts of the viewing experience turn casual watchers into loyal ones. With fast networks everywhere, over-the-top platforms compete on experience as much as content. Their 2026 study asked two hundred thirty users about convenience, interaction, emotional engagement, and service quality, then modeled how those shaped perceived value, satisfaction, and intention to keep using a service.

Smooth, easy use lifted value, satisfaction, and intention alike. Emotional experience helped on all three fronts too, partly by raising satisfaction. Service quality and functional value, though, did not directly drive intention; they worked only through satisfaction. Interactive features pushed intention directly. The practical lesson: platforms win loyalty when smooth performance and engaging content leave users satisfied, not merely impressed.
plos-pone-0350157:
Correction notice: Zhibin Yuan, Yuqi Gao, and co-authors issued this 2026 correction to their rat study of a gene regulator called MKL1 in lung hypertension caused by low oxygen. One panel in a main figure duplicated another by mistake, the chart beside it lacked axis labels, and some values in that chart were wrong. The notice supplies a corrected figure with the proper image from the original experiments and a fixed chart, plus fuller details of animal monitoring and humane endpoints.

The authors state the changes do not affect the results or conclusions. The original study reported that silencing the regulator calmed lung inflammation in this rat model of hypoxia-driven pulmonary hypertension. Underlying image and chart data for the corrected figure are shared with the notice.
plos-pone-0349757:
Sanjida Sultana Santa and colleagues measured heavy metals in soils beside an open landfill in Jashore, Bangladesh, where household and industrial waste are dumped together. They tested for eleven metals and converted the readings into standard risk indexes. Arsenic, mercury, cadmium, lead, zinc, copper, and manganese all stood out at levels of concern.

Open dumping is the usual practice in Bangladesh, so this one site stands for many. Comparing the metals' patterns helps separate what the landfill adds from what was already in the ground. Families farming and living near such dumps face the exposure directly. An index-based assessment like this turns raw chemistry into a ranked warning that local officials can act on.
plos-pone-0347557:
Dwita Rian Desandri and colleagues gathered the trials that test if gym-based heart rehab can shrink the fatty build-up in heart arteries, not just boost fitness. Drugs that lower blood fats are known to shrink this build-up, but the proof for exercise was spread thin. The team searched in 2025 and kept the trials that took scans of the arteries before and after rehab.

Five trials with two hundred seventeen patients fit, with plans built on hard interval work, steady aerobic work, and weights, all next to standard drug care. The plans cut the size of the build-up by a clear margin. If exercise truly shrinks artery build-up, rehab moves from a support act to a direct way to treat the disease.
plos-pone-0347957:
Xiaowei Luo and co-workers design a safer way to pick out gene-edited plants without leaving antibiotic resistance genes behind. Standard selection uses such markers, which raise safety worries. Their 2026 study gives tobacco a microbial gene that lets it break down biuret, a plant-harming by-product found in common fertilizer, and turns the poison into food.

On biuret feed, nearly four in five shoots carried the new gene, beating the standard method, and plants grew ready weeks sooner. Edited plants also shrugged off biuret at sprouting, even when nitrogen was scarce. In mixed pots, biuret cut weeds back hard while edited plants thrived. One chemical could thus select crops and suppress weeds at once.
plos-pone-0348357:
Daniel Oliveira dos Santos and his team probed a germ in wild opossums of Brazil. The germ, a strep type, was known from kin of these beasts in the north. Ten dead beasts were cut open for checks. Thirty-four live ones, caught in the wild, had their noses swabbed. Germ samples from the dead were grown and read gene by gene.

The germ showed in skin sores on the dead beasts. It also showed in the heart, the spleen, and the kidneys, a sign it can spread through the body. All live beasts tested clean. The germs bore no drug-shield genes and fell to most drugs. This is the first full sketch of the ill in these beasts.
plos-pone-0336457:
N. V. Satyanarayana and his team built a thin sheet that soaks up radar waves. It is printed on denim, so it bends. Most such sheets catch waves at one pitch. This one catches them at three. The sheet's face is a patch of copper shapes in mixed sizes. It was shaped in four rounds of work.

At each of its three pitches, the sheet drank in near all the waves that hit it. It did so at all wave twists. Bend tests showed it keeps its skill when curved. The team sees use in stealth, space links, and shield work for next-wave gear.
plos-pone-0343757:
Gabriel Bafunyembaka and colleagues study children in French Guiana who live with both sickle cell disease and asthma, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. The pairing is common and dangerous, since asthma raises the odds of painful crises and acute chest syndrome, the condition's deadliest complication.

Among one hundred thirty-eight children with confirmed asthma, nearly three-quarters had a severe course, defined by repeated hospitalizations for crises or chest syndrome in the previous year. Yet when the team tested many candidate factors together, none independently predicted severity. That negative result is itself useful: it warns clinicians in tropical settings not to rely on a simple checklist to guess which child will suffer most.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Congo crisis split the Council in September 1960. The new state's army had mutinied. Belgium sent troops back in. The Soviet Union and the West backed rival camps. At the 906th meeting, the big powers could not agree. Resolution 157 passed on 17 September 1960 by eight votes to two. Poland and the Soviet Union said no. France held back.

Blocked at home, the Council passed the file upward. It called a rare special session of the General Assembly. The tool came from the 1950 Uniting for Peace plan. That plan lets the Assembly act when vetoes freeze the Council. The session gave the wider membership its say on the Congo's fate.

Swaziland was among the last British lands in Africa to go free. King Sobhuza II took the throne of a free state on 6 September 1968. The small land, now called Eswatini, sat between South Africa and Mozambique. Its bid for a UN seat was filed as S/8808. Resolution 257 passed with no dissent on 11 September 1968.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Swaziland. The Assembly did so that month. The king would rule till 1982, one of the long reigns of the age. Landlocked and small, the state leaned hard on its big next-door state for trade. Still, its seat gave it a voice of its own. The text is the plain legal step that put one more African flag in the hall that fall.

Resolution 457 was adopted unanimously on 4 December 1979, a month after militants seized the United States embassy in Tehran. American diplomatic staff were being held hostage in Iran, and tension between the two countries was rising fast. The Council opened by voicing deep concern that the standoff could endanger wider peace and security.

Its central demand was direct: Iran must free the embassy personnel at once, protect them, and let them leave the country. The text also reminded all states of their duty to respect the safety of diplomats and embassy grounds under the Vienna Conventions. When Iran did not comply, the Council returned to the crisis within the month.

Resolution 1657, adopted on 6 February 2006, moves soldiers between two West African missions. The UN mission in Liberia, UNMIL, still had months left on its mandate. Next door, the operation in Côte d'Ivoire needed extra protection for UN personnel and property after attacks and unrest tied to the stalled peace process there.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the Secretary-General to redeploy at once up to one infantry company from Liberia to the Côte d'Ivoire operation, until 31 March 2006. The transfer was meant to give extra security coverage without prejudging later decisions about renewing the Ivorian operation. Inter-mission cooperation of this kind became a standard tool for UN commanders facing sudden local crises.

Resolution 1957, adopted on 15 December 2010, lifts a layer of the sanctions era from Iraq. Iraq's foreign minister had written that January confirming support for the non-proliferation regime and compliance with disarmament treaties. The UN atomic agency reported excellent cooperation from Baghdad on safeguards, and Iraq had begun applying the tougher Additional Protocol inspection rules in February 2010.

Rewarding that record, and acting under Chapter VII, the Council ended the weapons-related restrictions first imposed after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait. The step aimed to restore Iraq to the international standing it held before 1990. It closed the legal chapter opened by the disarmament demands that had dominated Iraq's relations with the UN for twenty years.

Bosnia's peace work is renewed in Resolution 1357. It passed by a full vote on 21 June 2001. The Council restated its faith in the Dayton peace pact of 1995. It thanked the many hands at work: the High Envoy, the NATO-led force, the UN team, and its police arm. States near Bosnia, it said, must play a fair part in the peace.

The UN team's term ran for twelve more months. The police task force went on with it. The world force that kept the truce won the same fresh span. The Council kept its yearly watch on the tests of peace: fair votes, the return of those who fled, and court action for war crimes.

Plunder of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's natural wealth is condemned in Resolution 1457, adopted on 24 January 2003. A Panel of Experts had reported on the illegal taking of resources and other riches during the war. The Council said this theft was a main force keeping the conflict alive, deepening the people's suffering, and holding back the country's growth.

The Council strongly condemns the illegal exploitation and demands that the states involved stop it at once. It says Congo's resources must be used openly, lawfully, and on fair terms for the Congolese people. It gives the panel a fresh six-month mandate to check its past findings, hear replies from those named, and advise on laws a transitional government could use to control the trade. States are urged to run their own inquiries, and Congo's move to suspend named officials is welcomed.

Congo's sanctions criteria are widened in Resolution 1857, adopted on 22 December 2008. The Group of Experts' 2008 reports traced embargo violations and the resource trade behind the eastern armed groups. The Council built on Resolution 1807 (2008) and on listing procedures from its other sanctions regimes. Those procedures include public reasons for listing and a delisting Focal Point.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms, transport, financial, and travel measures until 30 November 2009. It confirms the travel ban and asset freeze reach seven classes of designees: embargo violators, foreign armed-group leaders blocking disarmament, and externally backed militia leaders. They reach those recruiting or using children, those committing grave violations against children or women, those obstructing humanitarian aid, and those funding armed groups through illicit resource trade. The Group of Experts is extended to 30 November 2009, and the Committee must publish narrative summaries of listing reasons.

South Sudan's mission is extended through its first independence anniversary period in Resolution 2057, adopted in 2012. Intercommunal violence in Jonglei State had killed hundreds, cross-border clashes with Sudan had eased after Resolution 2046 (2012), and the new government was building institutions under an austerity budget.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, UNMISS, on its Resolution 1996 (2011) mandate through 15 July 2013. Protection of civilians and an improved security environment are the stated priorities, and UNMISS is authorized to use all necessary means for its protection tasks. Until the Joint Border Verification and Monitoring Mechanism starts, UNMISS must observe and report any flow of personnel or arms across the Sudan border. The Council welcomes the March 2012 action plan to end SPLA child recruitment and release all children in its ranks, and presses the government to end impunity and arbitrary detention.

Resolution 1757 is the Security Council decision of 30 May 2007. It brought the Special Tribunal for Lebanon into being. The tribunal was created to try those responsible for the 14 February 2005 bombing in Beirut. That bombing killed Lebanon's former prime minister and others. The tribunal was also to try connected attacks in Lebanon in the same period.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council ordered that the agreement between the United Nations and Lebanon take effect on 10 June 2007. Approval inside Lebanon had stalled. The long annex sets out the tribunal's makeup and its statute. The tribunal has Lebanese and international judges, a prosecutor, and a defence office.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/57 of the General Assembly deals with the health and environmental effects of weapons containing depleted uranium. Studies so far have not settled the long-term risks. The United Nations Environment Programme urges a precautionary approach because of uncertainties such as groundwater contamination. Noting both points, the Assembly asks the relevant agencies to update their research. States that used such munitions in conflicts are invited to share detailed information on where and how much was used. That way affected states can assess contaminated areas.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended for twelve months on 12 August 2004. The mission, created a year earlier, leads United Nations support for Iraqi institutions and representative government. It works through advice, training, and help with elections and law reform across the country. The Council said it would review the mandate in twelve months, or sooner if Iraq's government asked.

Fighting in Cyprus resumed in August 1974, in spite of the cease-fire the Council had demanded the month before. A second round of Turkish military action had opened on the island. Resolution 357 was adopted unanimously on 14 August 1974.

The Council deeply deplored the return to fighting. It reaffirmed Resolution 353 of July in all its parts. The parties were told to carry out those parts without delay. Everyone involved in the fighting had to stop all firing and military action at once. Talks had to restart without delay as well. Their aim was to restore peace in the area and constitutional government in Cyprus. The Council said it would stay ready to meet at once if the cease-fire broke down.

The United Nations mediator in Palestine was shot dead in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948. Count Folke Bernadotte, named in the text, died on his peace mission. The Council said the act seemed to be the work of a group of terrorists. Resolution 57, adopted the next day, records the response. The United Nations flag was to fly at half-mast for three days. The costs of the burial could be paid from the Working Capital Fund. Its president, or a deputy, would attend the burial.

Sweeping sanctions fell on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made up of Serbia and Montenegro, on 30 May 1992. Its authorities, including the Yugoslav People's Army, had ignored the demands of Resolution 752. That text had ordered a stop to the fighting and to outside interference in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Resolution 757 is the Council's answer.

All states had to block imports from the republic and stop exports to it. Its access to funds and other financial resources had to be cut off. The measures would last until Belgrade met the Council's demands. The sanctions built on the arms embargo first imposed in 1991. The text also deplored the forced expulsions aimed at changing the ethnic makeup of parts of Bosnia. The blocking of aid deliveries to Sarajevo and other towns was condemned as well.
un-sc-res-157:
The Congo crisis split the Council in September 1960. Its permanent members could not agree. That deadlock, the text says, stopped the Council from doing its chief job. On 17 September 1960 the Council chose a different route. It called an emergency special session of the General Assembly. The Uniting for Peace procedure allowed that move. The Assembly would make fitting recommendations on the Congo.

The session met within days as the crisis deepened. Congolese leaders were fighting for control of the new state. Foreign troops and advisers were already involved. The resolution is a twin of the Hungary step of 1956. Both show the Council handing a blocked crisis to the wider membership.
un-sc-res-457:
American diplomats were held hostage in Tehran when the Council acted in 1979. Embassy staff had been seized that November. On 4 December 1979 the Council voiced deep concern at the dangerous tension. It recalled its president's appeals of 9 and 27 November. Iran's foreign minister had set out his country's grievances in a letter. The Council said disputes must be settled by peaceful means under the Charter.

Iran had to release the embassy personnel at once. It had to protect them and let them leave the country. Iran and the United States had to work out their remaining issues peacefully. Both governments had to show the utmost restraint. The Secretary-General was asked to lend his good offices. The hostages in fact stayed captive for over a year.
un-sc-res-1657:
A company of peacekeepers was shifted from Liberia to Côte d'Ivoire by the Security Council on 6 February 2006. Côte d'Ivoire's crisis and the blocks on its peace process persisted from all sides. The Secretary-General had written on 1 February 2006 about the need. The United Nations Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, was due for renewal by 31 March 2006.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the Secretary-General to move up to one infantry company from UNMIL to the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire at once. The company would serve until 31 March 2006, adding security for United Nations staff and property. The move was without prejudice to later decisions on UNMIL's renewal or troop levels. The Council said it would review the arrangement within thirty days and by the March deadline. It also kept open the option of further transfers between the two missions.
un-sc-res-1357:
Bosnia's peace forces were renewed for another year on 21 June 2001. The Council restated its support for the Dayton Peace Agreement and for the High Representative's work. It thanked the stabilization force, the United Nations mission, and the international police for their service. The Bosnian authorities bore the first duty to make the peace work.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized the member states to keep the multinational stabilization force going for a planned twelve months. The force could take all measures needed to defend itself and carry out its mission. The United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, police task force included, was extended to 21 June 2002. The parties were reminded that they had pledged to cooperate fully with all bodies applying the agreement, the war crimes tribunal among them. The Council kept the Bosnian file under close review.
un-sc-res-1457:
Looting of natural wealth in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is taken up in Resolution 1457 of the United Nations Security Council, adopted on 24 January 2003. A panel of experts had reported that armed groups and foreign actors were stripping the country of resources. That trade, the panel found, helped keep the war going.

The text strongly condemns the illegal taking of Congo's resources and demands that states end it. It gives the expert panel six more months to check its findings and update its lists. People and firms named in the reports may reply, and their answers would be published. States are urged to run their own probes through their courts.
un-sc-res-1857:
With Resolution 1857, adopted on 22 December 2008, the Council turned to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Armed groups in the east lived off the illegal trade in minerals and timber. That trade paid for guns and kept the war going. Experts had traced how buyers abroad fed the chain without checking their sources.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the sanctions regime and its Group of Experts until 30 November 2009. It widens the travel bans and asset freezes to a new target class. Anyone backing illegal armed groups through the stolen resource trade can now be listed. So can those who block aid work. States should make sure firms handling Congolese minerals check their suppliers with care.
un-sc-res-2057:
South Sudan stood before the Council as it adopted Resolution 2057 on South Sudan in July 2012. The country had marked one year of independence from Sudan. Cross-border clashes with Sudan had eased but not ended. Fighting between communities in Jonglei state had killed hundreds and driven many from home.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the peacekeeping mission, called UNMISS, through 15 July 2013. Guarding civilians stays the mission's first task. It may use all necessary means within its reach to do so. The text presses Juba to fight corruption, end long detentions, and run disarmament well. It also asks the mission to watch the Sudan border and to report on Lord's Resistance Army attacks.
un-sc-res-1757:
When the Council met on 30 May 2007, it adopted Resolution 1757 on Lebanon. A huge bomb had killed the former prime minister, Rafiq Hariri, in February 2005. Lebanon and the United Nations had signed a deal to create a special court. Beirut's parliament could not ratify it, so the process stalled.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council puts the tribunal agreement into force on 10 June 2007. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon will try those behind the Hariri attack. It can also take linked attacks from the same period. The court mixes Lebanese and foreign judges and sits outside Lebanon. Voluntary gifts may cover any funding gap Beirut cannot pay.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
A fifth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/4857, reviews the force around 1960 and 1961. UNEF patrolled the Egypt-Israel frontier from its base in Gaza and Sinai posts. Its task was to keep a truce that neither side fully trusted.

The report covers the force's size, its daily patrol work, and minor incidents along the line. It also deals with funding, a sore point among member states from the start. These yearly reports form the paper trail of the first great peacekeeping force, in its steady middle years.
europmc-pmc10131557:
Solier and a large team identify a copper-based signaling pathway that drives inflammation and can be targeted by drugs, in a 2023 study. Inflammation defends the body against harm, but in excess it fuels diseases from sepsis to cancer. The team searched for fresh control points in this ancient system.

They found that copper inside certain immune cells helps switch on inflammatory programs. Blocking that copper signal calmed inflammation in their tests. The work names a new drug target in a pathway doctors have long wanted to control more precisely.
europmc-pmc10132957:
Ebrahimi and Samanta review how protein-based drugs are engineered through structural and chemical design, in a 2023 paper. Protein drugs have changed the treatment of cancer, diabetes, and immune disease. The authors note that proteins were set to make up half of the top-selling drugs of the year.

The review explains how scientists reshape proteins to bind better, last longer, and cause fewer side effects. It covers design guided by three-dimensional structure and by chemical tweaks. The paper shows how careful engineering turns natural proteins into precise medicines. It closes with open challenges in the field.
europmc-pmc10287557:
Okuzumi and a large team report that seeds of alpha-synuclein protein in blood serum can serve as markers for a family of brain diseases, in a 2023 study. These diseases, called synucleinopathies, include Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies. In each, alpha-synuclein folds wrongly and spreads through the brain in a seed-like way.

The team amplified those seeds from blood samples and read their shapes. Different diseases left distinct seed signatures that matched the clinical diagnosis. A blood test of this kind could ease diagnosis of diseases now confirmed mainly after death.
europmc-pmc10329457:
Finkel and co-authors asked in 2020 how microbes around plant roots shape root growth. Plants live amid a dense web of microbes that trade chemical signals. The team grew Arabidopsis, a small test plant, with a set of 185 bacterial strains. They then took the set apart to find which microbes changed the roots.

Finkel found that one genus, Variovorax, did the key work. It fully undid the strong block on root growth caused by many other strains. Variovorax did this by breaking down auxin, a plant hormone that guides growth. All of its known genomes carry the same gene set for that task. The result hints at ways to grow tougher crops.
europmc-pmc10412457:
Tsuboyama and co-authors measured in 2023 how stably a vast set of proteins fold. A protein must fold into a fixed shape to do its job. How much energy that fold holds shapes health, disease, and protein design. Past work could test just a few proteins at a time.

Their new method can test up to 900,000 protein parts in one week. In all, the team made 1.8 million measures and kept about 776,000 clean ones. The set covers each single change in 331 natural proteins and 148 designed ones. Tsuboyama used it to weigh how place and paired changes shift a fold. The data also showed where designed proteins miss the mark.
europmc-pmc10454957:
Onyeaka and co-authors reviewed in 2021 how Covid lockdowns changed daily life across the world. The World Health Organization named Covid-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Most nations then shut schools, shops, and travel to slow the virus. The team searched past studies for the full spread of effects.

Food access grew shaky as prices swung and supply lines broke. World output shrank, and tourism, hotels, and sport ground to a halt. School moved online, with gaps in who could join. Onyeaka also reports more strain on mental health and more abuse at home. One gain was cleaner air in many cities. The review urges planners to weigh all these costs next time.
europmc-pmc10618257:
Lee and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how fat-based carriers stir the immune system, and what that means for mRNA drugs. The carriers, lipid nanoparticles, ferry mRNA into cells for vaccines and cures. The body reads them as foreign, so they wake the innate immune arm. That wake-up then shapes the learned, adaptive response.

Some of that stir helps a vaccine work, Lee notes. Too much can cause side effects and blunt repeat doses. The review maps which parts of the carrier trigger which alarm. It also tracks the harm reports tied to that response. Ways to tune the stir up or down close the piece. Such tuning may raise both safety and strength of mRNA care.
europmc-pmc10790257:
Xu and co-authors offer a tool that keeps location in view when reading gene activity in tissue in this 2024 paper. Spatial transcriptomics is a method that measures which genes are active at many spots across a tissue slice. The location data helps show how cells are arranged and how they may signal each other. Older tools often lost that spatial detail or scaled poorly on sharp, high-detail datasets.

Their tool, SEDR, learns a compact summary of gene activity with a deep autoencoder, a network that squeezes data down and rebuilds it. A second network then weaves in the spot locations. SEDR grouped tissue regions more accurately than rival tools on standard test sets. It can also fill in missing gene readings and smooth out noise, the authors report.
europmc-pmc11059157:
Lee, Shin, and Chae review how cells choose what to pack into tiny export sacs in this 2024 paper. Exosomes are small sacs cells release to send proteins, fats, and gene messages to other cells. Their cargo decides where they act and what they do on arrival. How cells sort chosen cargo into the sacs is still not fully known.

The review gathers current insight on the sorting machinery for each cargo type. Membrane proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and signal molecules each follow distinct loading rules. The resulting sac contents shape cell growth, immune action, and disease spread. Cancer gets particular emphasis, since tumours use these sacs to aid growth. The authors argue that mastering cargo choice is essential for using sacs as disease markers and drug carriers.
europmc-pmc11128457:
Shi and colleagues review the Notch signal path in cancer and the drugs aimed at it in this 2024 paper. Notch signalling is an ancient cell-to-cell system that decides cell fates and builds organs. Its receptors and partners sit in cell membranes and must touch to fire the signal. In cancer the path can act as a driver or as a brake, depending on the tumour.

Faulty Notch signalling fuels cell shape change, vessel growth, invasion, and spread, the review says. It also keeps cancer cells in a stem-like state that resists chemotherapy. The path helps rewire how tumours burn fuel and shapes the tissue around them. That double role makes dosing tricky. The authors gather the mechanistic detail first, then survey targeted therapies. They argue that this full picture is crucial for designing smarter Notch drugs.
europmc-pmc11491057:
Wu, Zhang, Li, Wu, and Jiang explain the cold and hot tumour distinction and how to heat cold tumours in this 2024 paper. Immune checkpoint blockade frees T cells to attack cancer and has transformed treatment. Yet only a minority of patients respond. Responders usually show an inflamed, immune-active tumour, dubbed hot.

Non-responders often show a cold phenotype, an immune desert with few T cells inside. A third, excluded phenotype keeps T cells at the tumour's edge, between cold and hot. The review details the intrinsic tumour factors, immune traits, microenvironment features, and external factors that set each type. Distinguishing them is critical for predicting response, the authors argue. Targeted strategies to convert cold tumours toward hot are then surveyed. These include combinations that draw T cells in and strip away suppression.
europmc-pmc11718157:
GBD 2021 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators estimate the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2050, in this 2024 study. This resistance, where drugs stop working against bacteria, is a major global health challenge. A prior study quantified the burden for 2019. No study had yet paired historical trends with future forecasts for all places.

The team estimated deaths and years of healthy life lost, both caused by resistance and linked to it. Coverage spans 22 pathogens, 84 pathogen-drug pairings, and 11 infectious syndromes across 204 countries and territories. Inputs covered 520 million single records or isolates: death records, hospital discharges, lab germ data, literature studies, drug sales, and antibiotic use surveys among them. Age-specific and all-age figures were produced for each year.
europmc-pmc1363357:
Díaz-Uriarte and Alvarez de Andrés applied random forest methods to gene chip data in 2006. Gene selection seeks the smallest set that still predicts sample class. Older methods rank genes one by one with arbitrary cutoffs. Many handle only two classes at a time.

Random forest returns its own variable importance measures. It tolerates many noisy variables and few samples. Multi-class problems fit the method naturally. The authors propose a selection method built on those importance scores. Backward elimination trims genes while tracking prediction error. Díaz-Uriarte ties selection directly to the classifier itself.
europmc-pmc1393757:
Coller, Sang, and Roberts gave a new description of resting cells in 2006. Quiescence is a reversible halt in cell growth and division. It was assumed to be one uniform state. Human fibroblasts were driven to rest by three separate signals.

Gene profiling compared mitogen withdrawal, contact, and adhesion loss. Each signal switched its own unique gene set. Beneath the variety sat a shared quiescence program. Its genes enforce the halt and keep it reversible. One trick is suppressing terminal differentiation programs. Coller shows resting states differ by trigger yet share a core.
europmc-pmc1524957:
Silencing a gene fast helps test what it does. Bart and co-authors built such a system for rice in 2006, using protoplasts, plant cells stripped of their walls. Rice protoplasts were hard to prepare well. Their method uses young seedlings grown in the dark.

Reporter genes peaked about 20 hours after DNA delivery. Small plasmids entered 60 to 70 percent of cells. Short interfering RNAs, tiny RNA pieces that mute a target gene, cut reporter output by up to 83 percent within hours. Bart also made protoplasts from green leaf tissue. The system lets labs screen many rice genes quickly.
europmc-pmc1762357:
DNA barcoding trusts public databases, and that trust is shaky for fungi. Nilsson and co-authors audited fungal sequences in 2006 in the International Nucleotide Sequence Database. Species identification by sequence assumes entries are complete and correctly labeled.

Sampling of fungi was far from complete. About 20 percent of entries may be misidentified at species level. Most entries also lacked descriptive, up-to-date annotations. Nilsson warns the greatest challenges to barcoding are taxonomic, not technical. Fixing names and notes in the repositories matters as much as better sequencing.  The authors press database curators to clean up entries and fill the sampling gaps.
europmc-pmc1802757: Als3 is a Candida albicans invasin that binds to cadherins and induces endocytosis by host cells. — a 2005 science paper on a Candida invasion tool. It finds Als3 grabs cadherins. The paper is the Als3 study: the findings on Candida ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1817657: A specific primed immune response in Drosophila is dependent on phagocytes. — a 2005 science paper on fly immune priming. It finds phagocytes are needed. The paper is the priming study: the findings on Drosophila immunity, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1968657: Cytotoxic studies of paclitaxel (Taxol) in human tumour cell lines. — a 2005 science paper on Taxol cell killing. It studies the cytotoxic effects. The paper is the Taxol study: the findings on tumour ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2222957: The macaque gut microbiome in health, lentiviral infection, and chronic enterocolitis. — a 2005 science paper on macaque gut bugs. It maps the gut microbiome. The paper is the gut-bug study: the findings on macaque ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2265557: Recruitment to the nuclear periphery can alter expression of genes in human cells. — a 2005 science paper on nuclear-periphery gene effects. It finds the recruitment effects. The paper is the recruitment study: the findings on nuclear ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2360657: Clodronate-liposome-mediated depletion of tumour-associated macrophages: a new and highly effec — a 2008 science paper on bubble drugs that clear guards. It clears the guard cells for labs. The paper is the clear-out study: the notes on tumor ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2375057: Antagomir-17-5p abolishes the growth of therapy-resistant neuroblastoma through p21 and BIM. — a 2008 science paper on antagomir vs kid tumors. It kills the tumor growth for labs. The paper is the tumor-kill study: the notes on kid ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2376357: Association of perceived physician communication style with patient satisfaction, distress, can — a 2008 science paper on doctor-talk and patient mood. It links the communication style. The paper is the link study: the findings on patient ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2410157: Integrins: roles in cancer development and as treatment targets. — a 2008 science paper on integrins in cancer. It reviews the integrin roles. The paper is the integrin review: the findings on cancer, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2453157: Concentrations of the Sunscreen Agent Benzophenone-3 in Residents of the United States: Nationa — a 2008 science paper on sunscreen chemical levels. It measures the benzophenone levels. The paper is the measure study: the findings on sunscreen ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2515157: Evaluation of the bacterial diversity in the feces of cattle using 16S rDNA bacterial tag-encod — a 2008 science paper on cattle gut diversity. It evaluates the bacterial diversity. The paper is the diversity study: the findings on cattle ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2518857: A new perspective on Listeria monocytogenes evolution. — a 2008 science paper on Listeria's evolution story. It gives a new view for labs. The paper is the Listeria view: the findings on the germ's story, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2599757: Bisphenol A at environmentally relevant doses inhibits adiponectin release from human adipose t — a 2008 science paper on plastic-chemical doses. It tests the plastic doses for labs. The paper is the dose study: the notes on plastic ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2635757: Pretreatment of lignocellulosic wastes to improve ethanol and biogas production: a review. — a 2008 science paper on lignocellulosic pretreatment. It reviews the waste pretreatment. The paper is the pretreatment review: the findings on ethanol ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2654157: Myostatin inhibition in muscle, but not adipose tissue, decreases fat mass and improves insulin — a 2008 science paper on myostatin inhibition. It decreases the fat mass. The paper is the decrease study: the findings on myostatin ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2662657: Face mask use and control of respiratory virus transmission in households. — a 2008 science paper on face masks and virus transmission. It studies the mask control. The paper is the mask study: the findings on respiratory ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2706257: Expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in primary human breast cancer and breast cancer — a 2008 science paper on MMP expression. It expresses the matrix MMPs. The paper is the MMP study: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2711257: Prognostic indicators in hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review of 72 studies. — a 2008 science paper on liver-cancer warning signs. It lists the warning signs for labs. The paper is the sign study: the notes on liver ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2718857: Diagnostic accuracy of the vegetative and minimally conscious state: clinical consensus versus — a 2008 science paper on coma-scale hit rates. It grades the coma scales for labs. The paper is the grade study: the notes on coma ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2720457: Worth the 'EEfRT'? The effort expenditure for rewards task as an objective measure of motivatio — a 2008 science paper on the EEfRT task. It measures the effort expenditure. The paper is the EEfRT study: the findings on motivation ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2732457: Community-acquired Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia: global differences in clinical patterns. — a 2008 science paper on street-bug blood ills. It maps the street-bug ills for labs. The paper is the bug study: the notes on blood ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2763257: Structural, chemical and biological aspects of antioxidants for strategies against metal and me — a 2008 science paper on rust-fighter plans. It draws the rust-fighter plans for labs. The paper is the plan study: the notes on rust ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2780357: SOS response induces persistence to fluoroquinolones in Escherichia coli. — a 2008 science paper on SOS persistence. It induces the fluoroquinolone persistence. The paper is the persistence study: the findings on E. coli ills, filed here in full session today.
jonston-history-wonderful-things-nature-:
John Jonston's History of the Wonderful Things of Nature came out in English in 1657. Its Latin original bore the grand title Thaumatographia naturalis, a writing of nature's wonders. Jonston collected marvels the way other scholars collected coins or books, eagerly and at length.

Monsters, prodigies, and strange births fill the volume. Jonston draws cases from every corner of the known world and from authors old and new. A comet, a two-headed calf, and a rain of blood all count as nature speaking. The Renaissance loved a wonder, and this book fed that love. It also shows how thin the line then ran between science and sign-reading.
lycosthenes-prodigiorum-chronicon-1557:
Conrad Lycosthenes, a Swiss scholar, published his Chronicle of Prodigies in 1557. The Latin book gathers omens and wonders from Creation down to his own year. It is among the most richly pictured prodigy books of the Renaissance, a chronicle in which history itself becomes a book of signs.

Monstrous births, sea monsters, and wonders in the sky mark the turning years. Comets and strange rains appear beside the falls of kings. Lycosthenes drew on ancient historians and on fresh reports alike. His readers learned to scan the past for God's warnings. The chronicle taught Europe to read events, bodies, and skies as one long message.
plos-pone-0004957:
People often seek expert financial advice under uncertainty. Jan Engelmann and colleagues asked what that advice does inside the brain. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They scanned volunteers making risky financial decisions. Some decisions came with an expert's recommendation.

Advice effectively offloaded the decision work. Brain activity for weighing risk quieted when a recommendation was available. Neuroeconomics had mapped risky choice in depth before this. The neural effect of external advice was largely unknown. The study gives a brain-level account of advice. It helps explain why following an advisor can feel like relief.
plos-pone-0005057:
Prions are deadly proteins that spread between cells. Their route from infection sites to the brain was not clear. Vincenzo Mattei and colleagues found a possible vehicle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells shed tiny bubbles from their membranes. These microvesicles carry cargo to neighboring cells.

The bubbles carried the normal prion protein, PrPC. They also propagated prion infectivity to other cells. The microvesicles act like taxis for the disease. That reveals a new vehicle for prion spread. Blocking the bubbles might slow the disease. The finding also matters beyond prions. Membrane bubbles move many kinds of cargo, and this study shows their dark side.
plos-pone-0005157:
A simple blood draw could reveal disease biomarkers. Reading gene activity from whole blood is the route. Technical noise has plagued that route, though. Ze Tian and colleagues built a practical platform in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used global gene expression profiling of peripheral whole blood. Their aim was a platform ready for biomarker studies.

The platform tames the technical factors that distort results. Standardized steps make profiles comparable across experiments. Blood biomarkers could serve many diseases at once. Reliability is what the field lacked. This work turns a messy method into a usable tool. Later biomarker claims stand on such groundwork. Without it, promising markers fail to replicate.
plos-pone-0005257:
When insulin calls, fat cells move a sugar transporter called GLUT4 to their surface to take in glucose. Small switch proteins of the Rab family help run that traffic. Kaddai and colleagues identified one more switch, Rab4b, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Rab4a was already known to help control GLUT4 in fat cells. The team found fat cells also make Rab4b and that it shares control of GLUT4 placement. Each added gear in this traffic system is a possible factor in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Each new switch in this chain is one more place where a drug might help fat cells take in sugar when insulin alone can no longer do it.
plos-pone-0005357:
Cystic fibrosis is caused by faults in the cftr gene and brings airway inflammation with stubborn Pseudomonas infections. Tracheal glands, small glands in the windpipe, may play a specific part in that process. Bastonero and colleagues compared those glands in normal and CF cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study found new microbicidal functions for tracheal glands, ways they kill microbes directly. In cystic fibrosis, that anti-infectious response to Pseudomonas aeruginosa is defective. A broken gland defense helps explain why CF airways cannot clear this germ. Thick mucus gets the blame in this disease, but glands that fail to kill germs are a fault of a kind. And one that may be open to a drug in its own right.
plos-pone-0005957:
Sarin is a nerve gas that jams a vital enzyme and can kill within minutes. Fredrik Ekström, Andreas Hörnberg, Elisabet Artursson and colleagues studied an antidote called HI-6 in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The jammed enzyme is acetylcholinesterase, which the body needs to end nerve signals, and HI-6 is built to free it.

Using X-ray methods and computer models, the team solved the shape of HI-6 bound to the poisoned enzyme. That shape shows how the rescue works at the level of single atoms. A clear view of the rescue step guides the design of better antidotes, work that serves both medicine and defense against chemical weapons.
plos-pone-0006057:
A tumor sample is never pure tumor, and that mix can skew every measurement made from it. Hanna Göransson, Karolina Edlund, Maria Rydåker and colleagues built a correction in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses SNP array data from clinical lung cancer samples to estimate the normal cell fraction. It also spots regions where one gene copy is lost yet the total count stays two.

That second pattern, copy-neutral loss, hides from cruder tests. Measuring both lets labs read a tumor's true genome through the normal cells mixed in. The method sharpens cancer genomics where it matters most: in real patient samples, not in pure cell lines grown in a dish.
plos-pone-0006157:
Donor marrow cells can help a patient rebuild blood without taking over the marrow themselves. Stephan Fricke, Manuela Ackermann, Alexandra Stolzing and colleagues tested that helping role in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies non-adherent bone marrow derived cells, a population that can give rise to several mesenchymal cell types and aids tissue regeneration.

The donor cells facilitated hematopoietic recovery but did not lead to donor engraftment, the title reports. Help without takeover is an attractive profile for transplant support, since lasting foreign engraftment carries its own risks. The mouse results guide strategies that borrow donor cells' support while keeping the patient's own blood system in charge.
plos-pone-0006257:
Imatinib transformed treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia, but resistance and late-stage disease remain problems. Zheng Hu and colleagues tested whether proteasome inhibitors, drugs that block the cell's protein shredder, boost imatinib, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Low-dose imatinib combined with such blockers was the combination on trial.

The two drug types worked in synergy against leukemia cells, the authors report. Combining them may help patients whose disease no longer answers imatinib alone. Heart side effects linked to imatinib also motivate lower-dose strategies. The study supports trials of the pairing in harder phases of the disease.
plos-pone-0006657:
Reto Baertschiger and co-authors tested stromal cells in injured liver in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multipotent mesenchymal stromal cells are currently investigated clinically as cellular therapy for a variety of diseases. Differentiation of these cells toward endodermal lineages raised hope they could rebuild liver. The team examined the fibrogenic potential of human cells in injured liver.

Fibrogenic means scar-forming, the opposite of what therapy wants. Their title flags that potential directly. Testing for harm is as important as testing for benefit in cell therapy. The study tempers enthusiasm with a concrete safety question.
plos-pone-0006757:
Marie-Cécile Caillaud and colleagues watched checkpoint proteins at work in dividing plant cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The spindle assembly checkpoint guards chromosome division. It blocks segregation until chromosomes attach properly to the spindle. That surveillance prevents cells gaining or losing chromosomes. Most checkpoint knowledge came from animals and yeast, not plants.

The team characterized checkpoint protein dynamics in plants. Some roles matched those known in other organisms. Others were conserved in form but unsuspected in function. Plants divide differently, with no centrioles and open cell walls forming. Their checkpoint adaptations reflect those differences. The work widens the checkpoint story across the tree of life.
plos-pone-0006857:
Oliver J. Sabot and colleagues piloted a global malaria drug subsidy in rural Tanzania in PLOS ONE in 2009. Only a small share of fever patients used recommended combination therapies. High retail prices were a major reason. Many patients buy treatment from private drug shops. A global subsidy for artemisinin-based combinations was proposed to cut prices.

The pilot distributed subsidized therapies through private drug shops. The team measured the impact on availability, price, and use. Subsidies that work in shops can reach patients clinics miss. The results inform whether a worldwide subsidy deserves launch. Malaria policy depends on evidence like this from real markets.
plos-pone-0006957:
Maritza Jaramillo, Marie-Josée Bellemare, Caroline Martel, and others studied malaria pigment in PLOS ONE in 2009. As malaria parasites digest blood, they leave a dark pigment called hemozoin. More and more work tied this pigment to immune harm in malaria. One point was still in dispute. Could pure pigment alone stir the immune system, with no other parasite parts mixed in?

The team made hemozoin-like crystals in the lab. They matched the crystals' shape and effects against the real pigment. The lab-made crystals did switch on immune responses. That answer matters, since the pigment may be a target for easing the worst harms of malaria.
plos-pone-0007057:
Adrián Granada and Hanspeter Herzel asked how rhythms lock on quickly in PLOS ONE in 2009. Entrainment is the process where oscillators sync to an outside signal. It appears everywhere in nature, from fireflies to brain waves. The time taken to sync up matters in many living processes.

The pair studied a generic oscillator model. They searched its dynamics for what makes entrainment fast. Slow settling can mean missed signals in real biological clocks. Their results give design rules for rhythms that must lock on swiftly, from circadian clocks to neural circuits.
plos-pone-0007157: Wei Song, Avima Ruder, Liangyuan Hu, and colleagues examined the genetic epidemiology of glioblastoma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study covered human leukocyte antigen alleles and motifs, the immune identity markers people inherit. It reported findings that confirm earlier results and added new ones. Work of this kind tests whether immune system genes shape the risk of this aggressive brain tumor.
plos-pone-0007257:
Zahirul Islam, Alex van Belkum, Jaap A. Wagenaar, and colleagues compared bacterial strains from paralysis patients in Bangladesh in 2009. Campylobacter jejuni commonly causes acute gastroenteritis, or gut infection. It is also linked to later nerve disorders such as Guillain-Barré syndrome and Miller Fisher syndrome, which can paralyze patients.

The authors genotype dozens of C. jejuni strains from Bangladeshi patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome. Comparative genotyping shows which strain features cluster with the syndrome. Their work may reveal why only some gut infections trigger severe nerve damage afterward. It also builds regional data where such studies are scarce.
plos-pone-0007357:
Colin K. Franz, Eric T. Quach, Christina A. Krudy, and colleagues tested nerve injury effects in a rat model of ALS in 2009. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes muscle weakness and wasting through progressive motoneuron loss. Before motoneurons die, their junctions with muscle fail and axons retract, cutting muscles off from nerve control early in disease.

Effective treatment will need to protect those junctions. The authors apply a conditioning lesion, a prior nerve injury, in the rat model. They report selective protection from that lesion. Their PLOS ONE result suggests injury signals can activate defenses in vulnerable motoneurons.
openalex-w2121408857: Lithium helps many bipolar patients — predicting who is hard. A 2013 review studied response to lithium maintenance in bipolar disorder. The work compared past and future methods amid variable treatment lengths — a clinician's guide, reviewed in full detail.
openalex-w2131618757: Mangrove mud hides a microbial world. A 2012 survey read the DNA of Brazilian mangrove sediments. The 215-Mb dataset opened the sediment's microbial life and metabolism — mud's code, read at last for science and all — mangroves' hidden life.
openalex-w2145725157: Plants fight stress with antioxidant enzymes. A 2012 review covers ascorbate peroxidase's role in plant defense. The work traced how the enzyme detoxifies hydrogen peroxide under stress — plants' shield, explained at last for botanists now.
plos-pone-0006357:
People who have never seen numbers still handle them with familiar quirks. Elena Salillas and colleagues studied numerical tasks in blind participants in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Blind people perform similarly to sighted people on number comparison and parity judgments, especially with sounds instead of sights.

Surprisingly, the blind show the same spatial effects in their number judgments. Numbers seem to be laid out along a mental line even without vision. That result suggests the number sense does not depend on visual experience. It informs how maths should be taught to blind students.
openalex-w2288397357: Paying landowners to protect forests and watersheds sounds simple — but does it work? This 2016 PLoS ONE meta-study systematizes 55 payments-for-environmental-services schemes worldwide into a quantitative database. Comparing these conditional payment programs reveals global patterns in how they're designed and what they achieve, offering lessons for conservation policy.
openalex-w2341640557: Making sperm is one of biology's most intricate productions, running three gene-expression programs at once: cell division, meiosis, and the final sculpting of sperm. This 2016 study profiles gene activity in highly purified mouse spermatogenic cells, catching the moment the program switches from meiotic to post-meiotic genes. The signatures illuminate how testes orchestrate this complex differentiation.
openalex-w2391304757: Psychologists constantly ask: how many underlying dimensions does a questionnaire really measure? This 2017 PLoS ONE paper introduces exploratory graph analysis, a new approach to estimating the number of dimensions, and pits it against classics like parallel analysis and Kaiser's eigenvalue rule. The comparison shows where the new method shines in realistic conditions.
openalex-w2508274757: Cleaning water with sunlight needs catalysts that work in visible light — and this 2016 Scientific Reports paper builds one. The team synthesizes zinc oxide/cerium oxide nanocomposites by thermal decomposition, using cerium ions to unlock visible-light photocatalysis. X-ray spectroscopy confirms the chemistry; the tests show the composite breaks down pollutants and doubles as an electrochemical material.
openalex-w2808973857: Alcohol raises blood pressure — but genes modulate how much. This 2018 PLoS ONE genome-wide study of up to 570,000 people across ancestries hunts for novel blood-pressure associations that appear only when gene-alcohol interactions are modeled. The approach uncovers genetic signals that simpler analyses miss.
openalex-w2921342657: Tracking antibiotic resistance worldwide is hard — but sewers offer a shortcut. This 2019 Nature Communications paper analyzes untreated sewage from 79 sites in 60 countries, using metagenomics to map the bacterial resistome. The approach yields representative resistance data for healthy populations that clinics alone could never provide.
openalex-w2965771657: Jets containing b-hadrons are gold for physicists — they flag top quarks and Higgs decays. This 2019 European Physical Journal C paper presents the b-jet identification algorithms ATLAS used in Run 2, evaluating their performance in simulation and measuring efficiency with top-quark pair events at 13 TeV. The taggers underpin precision LHC physics.
openalex-w3013358557: Liver injuries are among trauma's most frequent life-threatening wounds. This 2020 World Journal of Emergency Surgery paper delivers the WSES guidelines: anatomy, hemodynamics, and associated injuries determine the strategy. The consensus standardizes care when seconds count.
openalex-w3038797657: Do hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle affect athletic performance? This 2020 Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis examines the evidence in eumenorrheic women. The conflicting data get a rigorous synthesis — with no consensus yet, but better questions.
europmc-pmc2803857: BLAST, the workhorse for searching DNA and protein databases, got a major rewrite described in this 2009 paper. The authors present BLAST+, rebuilt with a cleaner architecture for speed and flexibility. They explain the new design and show what the suite can do. The paper documents the version of BLAST that still powers sequence searches in labs worldwide.
europmc-pmc2816657: Low oxygen makes breast cancer more aggressive, and this 2010 paper uncovers part of how. The authors show hypoxia boosts Notch signaling, which lowers E-cadherin and lets cancer cells migrate and invade more freely. The chain links oxygen starvation to metastasis. Blocking this pathway became a candidate strategy against spreading tumors.
europmc-pmc2846857: Animal stroke research looked more promising than it was. This 2010 paper shows publication bias in animal stroke studies leads to major overstatement of treatment efficacy, because negative results go unpublished. The authors quantify the inflation. Their exposé forced the field to confront its own skewed literature.
europmc-pmc2852857: Grapes pack color compounds tied to health claims. This 2010 review sifts what grape polyphenols do in the body. The authors stack the proof, from heart to cell defense, and judge its strength. Their take gives the fruit's fame a firm base without overstating what the science shows.
europmc-pmc2854757: Flame-guard dust coats homes, and this 2010 paper asks what it does to men. The team tied house dust's organophosphate compounds to hormone levels and sperm health. Their read found dips where dust ran high. The tie put home dust on the male-health map.
europmc-pmc2916857: Nerve cells branch like trees, and this 2010 paper finds one rule for them all. The authors propose a general theory of neuronal branching with practical application to real neurons. Their single rule predicts diverse arbors across cell types. The work unified a sprawling field with elegant math.
europmc-pmc2958657: Resting cells are busier than they look. This 2010 paper finds quiet fibroblasts still burn fuel at a high rate. The authors topple the idle-cell myth. Their work reframes what cellular rest means. Even parked cells keep their engines warm.
europmc-pmc2965757: Extreme blood pressure runs in genes, and this 2010 study finds a culprit. The authors' genome-wide study of blood pressure extremes identifies a variant near UMOD linked to hypertension. Their find points to kidney handling of salt. The work opened a therapeutic lead.
europmc-pmc3000457: Disease markers in blood need measuring at scale. This 2010 paper brings a DNA-tag method that reads thousands of proteins from one sample. The authors' platform powers marker hunts. Their work spread through clinics. One drop of blood now yields a protein portrait.
europmc-pmc3029257: Pseudomonas slime cities lean on a sugary scaffold. This 2011 paper shows the Pel sugar gives Pseudomonas biofilms their structure and shield. The authors reveal the scaffold. Their work points to slime-busting drugs. Lung infections in cystic fibrosis use this shield.
europmc-pmc3037057: Trial lotteries need unpredictable blocks. This 2011 paper explains how random block sizes keep treatment assignment secret. The author's method guards trials against peeking. Their guidance spread through trial design. Fixed blocks let doctors guess the next patient. Random blocks close the guessing loophole.
europmc-pmc3041657: Venn diagrams got beautiful and programmable. This 2011 paper introduces VennDiagram, an R package for highly-customizable Venn and Euler diagrams.
